guides.title: Semantics — The Study of Meaning
guides.summary: A full survey of semantics: how words and sentences carry meaning, how meanings combine, and how linguists model reference, truth, ambiguity, quantification, tense, implicature and metaphor.

sections.heading: What Semantics Studies, and Why It Matters
sections.body:
Semantics is the study of meaning in language: what words mean, how their meanings combine into the meaning of a phrase or sentence, and how those meanings connect to the world people talk about. It sits between two neighbours. On one side is syntax, which describes the shapes sentences may take without asking what they say; the classic demonstration is Noam Chomsky's 1957 sentence "Colourless green ideas sleep furiously", which is perfectly well formed and yet semantically deviant. On the other side is pragmatics, which studies what a speaker manages to convey on a particular occasion over and above what the words strictly encode. Semantics is the middle layer: the stable, conventional contribution that a competent speaker knows simply by knowing the language.

The reason this matters practically is that meaning is where language does its work. A contract, a dosage label, a legal statute, a safety instruction and a line of code all fail in the same way when their semantics is underdetermined. The 1999 loss of NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter is often cited as a units error, and it was, but at root it was a semantic failure: two teams used the same numeral to mean pound-seconds and newton-seconds respectively. Ambiguity in a will or an insurance clause has decided real inheritances and real payouts. Semantics gives us the vocabulary to say precisely where such a failure lives.

Semantics also matters because it is the part of language that most resists the idea that meaning is simply a private mental image. If meaning were a picture in the head, no two people would ever mean the same thing, and translation would be impossible. Yet people successfully coordinate on meanings across enormous differences of experience. A person blind from birth uses the word "red" in ways that align with sighted usage in almost every inferential respect: they know that red is a colour, that a thing cannot be uniformly red and uniformly green, that ripe tomatoes are red. Whatever meaning is, it must be something public enough to be shared and learned.

The field has three broad research programmes that recur throughout its history. Formal or truth-conditional semantics, descending from Gottlob Frege and given linguistic form by Richard Montague in the late 1960s, models meaning in terms of the conditions under which sentences are true. Cognitive semantics, associated with George Lakoff, Ronald Langacker and Eleanor Rosch, models meaning in terms of mental structures such as prototypes, image schemas and frames. Distributional semantics, whose slogan comes from J. R. Firth's 1957 remark that "you shall know a word by the company it keeps", models meaning statistically from patterns of co-occurrence in large text corpora, and now underpins essentially all machine language technology. These programmes are frequently presented as rivals. They are better understood as answering different questions about the same phenomenon, and a serious student of meaning eventually needs all three.

sections.heading: Sense, Reference, and the Puzzle That Started Modern Semantics
sections.body:
The single most productive distinction in semantics was drawn by the German logician Gottlob Frege in an 1892 paper, "Uber Sinn und Bedeutung" ("On Sense and Reference"). Frege noticed a puzzle so simple it is easy to miss. The ancient Babylonians had two names for the planet Venus: Phosphorus, the morning star, and Hesperus, the evening star. Both names pick out the same object. So the statement "Hesperus is Phosphorus" and the statement "Hesperus is Hesperus" should say exactly the same thing, since the parts refer to the same things. Yet the first was a genuine astronomical discovery and the second is a triviality nobody could learn anything from. Something about the names differs, even though what they pick out does not.

Frege's answer was to split meaning in two. The reference (Bedeutung) of a name is the object it picks out. The sense (Sinn) is the mode of presentation, the particular way the object is given to us. "Hesperus" presents Venus as the bright body seen in the west after sunset; "Phosphorus" presents the same body as the one seen in the east before dawn. Same reference, different senses, and it is the difference in sense that makes the identity statement informative. Frege extended the scheme to whole sentences: the sense of a sentence is the thought it expresses, and its reference, startlingly, is its truth value, either the True or the False.

The sense-reference split does an enormous amount of work. It explains why substituting co-referring terms can change meaning inside contexts such as belief reports. From "Lois believes Superman can fly" and the fact that Superman is Clark Kent, it does not follow that Lois believes Clark Kent can fly, because belief attaches to senses rather than to bare objects. Contexts where substitution fails are called opaque or intensional, and they include belief, knowledge, hope, necessity and quotation. Contexts where substitution is safe are called transparent or extensional.

The distinction also lets us handle terms with a sense but no reference. "The present King of France", "unicorn" and "the largest prime number" are perfectly meaningful, which they could not be if meaning simply were reference. Bertrand Russell's 1905 paper "On Denoting" gave a rival treatment, analysing "The present King of France is bald" as a triple claim: there is at least one King of France, there is at most one, and he is bald. On Russell's analysis the sentence is straightforwardly false rather than meaningless. Peter Strawson objected in 1950 that ordinary speakers do not judge it false but rather feel the question does not arise, which pointed toward the modern notion of presupposition. That dispute, over a hundred and twenty years old, remains live, and every contemporary theory of definite descriptions is recognisably a descendant of one of the two positions.

sections.heading: Compositionality: How Small Meanings Build Large Ones
sections.body:
A speaker of English can understand a sentence never previously encountered, such as "The librarian who fed my neighbour's tortoise resigned on Tuesday." No one memorised that sentence. The capacity to understand it must come from knowing the meanings of the parts and the rules for combining them. This is the principle of compositionality, usually attributed to Frege though he never stated it in that form: the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its constituents and the way they are syntactically combined.

Compositionality is a constraint on theories rather than an obvious fact about language, and its force is that it makes language learnable and productive with finite resources. A vocabulary of perhaps 40,000 to 60,000 words for an educated adult, plus a modest set of combinatorial rules, generates an unbounded set of interpretable sentences. Without compositionality, understanding a new sentence would require having stored its meaning in advance, and the number of sentences of twenty words or fewer already exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe.

The principle immediately explains structural ambiguity. "Old men and women" has two readings because the adjective can attach to "men" alone or to the whole conjunction; the words are identical and only the bracketing differs. "I saw the man with the telescope" splits according to whether the prepositional phrase modifies the verb or the noun. Newspaper headlines exploit the same mechanism unintentionally: "Squad helps dog bite victim" is funny only because two different structures assign two different meanings to one string. If meaning were not built up from structure, these ambiguities would be inexplicable.

The hard cases are the interesting ones. Idioms such as "kick the bucket", "spill the beans" and "by and large" appear to violate compositionality outright, since knowing the parts does not give you the whole. The standard response is that an idiom is a single lexical item that happens to be spelled with spaces, though this is complicated by the fact that many idioms remain internally flexible: one can say "the beans were spilled" but not "the bucket was kicked" with the idiomatic meaning, which suggests idioms vary in how tightly frozen they are. Adjectives create a second family of problems. "Red car" is straightforward, but "former senator" denotes someone who is not a senator, "alleged murderer" leaves the question open, and "small elephant" describes something enormous by absolute standards. These non-intersective adjectives are handled by treating them as functions that operate on the noun's meaning rather than as properties intersected with it.

The practical payoff is that compositionality is what makes systematic translation, parsing and inference possible at all. Every programming language is rigidly compositional by design, which is precisely why a compiler can determine the meaning of a program it has never seen. Natural language is compositional to a first approximation and messily so at the edges, and mapping exactly where the mess lies is much of the day-to-day work of the field.

sections.heading: Truth Conditions and the Model-Theoretic Method
sections.body:
The dominant formal approach to sentence meaning identifies meaning with truth conditions. To know what "The kettle is boiling" means is not to know whether it is true; it is to know what the world would have to be like for it to be true. This idea traces to the Polish logician Alfred Tarski, who in 1933 gave a rigorous definition of truth for formal languages, and to Donald Davidson, who argued in a celebrated 1967 paper that a theory of meaning for a natural language could take the form of a Tarski-style truth theory.

Tarski's schema is deceptively plain: the sentence "snow is white" is true if and only if snow is white. The left-hand side mentions a sentence; the right-hand side uses language to describe the world. A full theory generates one such biconditional for every sentence of the language, and does so recursively from a finite base. For a simple predicate-logic fragment the recursion runs roughly as follows. A name denotes an individual in the domain. A one-place predicate denotes a set of individuals. An atomic sentence formed from a name and a predicate is true if and only if the individual denoted is a member of the set denoted. A conjunction is true if and only if both conjuncts are. A negation is true if and only if its argument is not. And so on, upward, for arbitrarily complex sentences.

The machinery is called model-theoretic because it evaluates sentences relative to a model: a set of individuals called the domain, plus an interpretation function assigning denotations to the vocabulary. A tiny worked model makes it concrete. Let the domain be three people, Ana, Ben and Cara. Let "sings" denote the set containing Ana and Cara, and "dances" the set containing Cara alone. Then "Ana sings" is true, "Ben sings" is false, "Cara sings and Cara dances" is true, and "Everyone who dances sings" is true because the only dancer is in the singing set. Changing the model changes the truth values, exactly as changing the world would.

The great extension came from possible-worlds semantics, developed by Saul Kripke, Jaakko Hintikka, David Lewis and others from the late 1950s onward. Instead of a single model, we consider a whole space of them, each representing a way things might be. An intension is then a function from worlds to extensions. The intension of "the tallest person alive" picks out different individuals in different worlds; its extension in ours is one specific person. Necessity becomes truth at every accessible world, possibility truth at some. Richard Montague's papers of 1970 to 1973, especially "The Proper Treatment of Quantification in Ordinary English", showed that this apparatus could be applied to English directly, and effectively founded formal semantics as a linguistic discipline.

The approach has real limits worth stating plainly. It says nothing about imperatives or questions without extension, since neither is true or false. It treats all necessary truths as having the same meaning, so that "2 plus 2 equals 4" and "every square has four sides" come out identical, a well-known granularity problem nobody has fully solved.

sections.heading: Lexical Semantics: What Is Inside a Word
sections.body:
Sentence meaning is built from word meaning, so any complete semantics needs an account of the lexicon. Lexical semantics asks what a single word contributes, how that contribution is structured internally, and how the several thousand core words of a language relate to one another.

The oldest analytic strategy is decomposition into semantic features, borrowed from phonology in the 1960s by Jerrold Katz and Jerry Fodor. On this view "man" is roughly HUMAN, ADULT, MALE, and "woman" differs only in the last feature. Decomposition captures real regularities: it explains why "bachelor" entails "unmarried", why "kill" entails "die", and why "My sister is a man" feels contradictory rather than merely unlikely. But strict feature analysis famously struggles with the boundaries. Ludwig Wittgenstein's discussion of the word "game" in the Philosophical Investigations, published in 1953, pointed out that board games, ball games, solitaire and ring-a-ring-o'-roses share no single feature; they form a family resemblance, a network of overlapping similarities like the strands of a rope, none running its whole length.

A more successful decompositional programme works on verbs. Verbs can be analysed into event templates built from a small set of primitives such as CAUSE, BECOME, ACT and STATE. "Break" as in "The vase broke" is BECOME broken; "break" as in "Ali broke the vase" is CAUSE to BECOME broken. This predicts a great deal: which verbs alternate between transitive and intransitive uses, which allow the resultative construction ("hammer the metal flat"), and why "The vase broke" is fine while "The vase cut" is not. James Pustejovsky's Generative Lexicon, developed in the 1990s, adds a qualia structure recording what a thing is made of, what it is for, and how it comes about, which explains why "begin the book" is understood as beginning to read or write it, since reading and writing are the book's telic and agentive qualia.

A useful contrast is between denotation and connotation. "Deceased", "dead" and "snuffed it" have close to identical denotations, but they carry different registers, attitudes and social signals. Connotation is not decoration; it does real communicative work, and word choice here is what makes the difference between a clinical report, a news bulletin and an insult.

Finally, lexical meaning is not fully fixed. Semantic change is continuous and follows recognisable pathways: broadening, as with "dog", which once named a specific breed; narrowing, as with "meat", which meant food in general and survives in "sweetmeat"; amelioration, as with "nice", which meant ignorant in Middle English via Latin nescius; and pejoration, as with "silly", which meant blessed. Metaphorical extension is the commonest engine of all, taking "grasp" from the hand to the mind and "crane" from the bird to the machine. Any dictionary is a snapshot of a moving target.

sections.heading: Sense Relations: How Words Hang Together
sections.body:
Words do not carry meaning in isolation; they occupy positions in a network, and much of what a speaker knows about a word is how it relates to its neighbours. Mapping these relations is the structural core of lexical semantics and the organising principle behind thesauruses and machine-readable lexicons such as WordNet, built at Princeton from 1985 under George Miller and containing roughly 155,000 words grouped into about 117,000 sets of synonyms.

Synonymy is sameness of meaning, and strict synonymy is rare. "Begin" and "commence" differ in formality; "couch" and "sofa" differ regionally; "sea" and "ocean" differ in scale. A practical test is substitutability: two words are synonymous to the degree that swapping them preserves truth conditions across contexts. Nearly always some context breaks the swap, which is why editors distrust the thesaurus.

Antonymy is more structured than it looks and comes in at least three kinds. Gradable antonyms, such as hot and cold or big and small, lie on a scale with a middle ground, so denying one does not assert the other; something can be neither hot nor cold. Complementary antonyms, such as alive and dead or pass and fail, exhaust the space, so denying one does assert the other. Converse or relational antonyms, such as buy and sell, parent and child, above and below, describe the same situation from opposite ends, so that "A sold B to C" and "C bought B from A" are two descriptions of one event.

Hyponymy is the is-a relation of inclusion. A spaniel is a kind of dog, a dog a kind of mammal, a mammal a kind of animal. The more general term is the hypernym. Hyponymy is what licenses inference: from "I saw a spaniel" it follows that I saw an animal. It is also asymmetric and transitive, which makes it the backbone of any taxonomy or ontology. Meronymy is the part-of relation: wheel to car, petal to flower, chapter to book. Unlike hyponymy it is not reliably transitive, since a nail is part of a finger and a finger part of a hand, but calling a nail part of the hand is at best strained.

Two further relations matter for real usage. Collocation is the tendency of particular words to co-occur beyond chance: one makes a decision but takes a decision in British English, and strong tea is idiomatic while powerful tea is not, despite the near-synonymy. Collocational knowledge is a large part of what separates a fluent non-native speaker from a native one, and it is almost invisible to introspection. Semantic fields group words covering a conceptual domain, such as the vocabulary of cooking or of kinship, and comparing fields across languages is one of the sharpest tools available for seeing how differently languages carve up the same territory.

sections.heading: Ambiguity, Vagueness, and Polysemy: Three Different Problems
sections.body:
Everyday talk lumps together several very different ways in which language can fail to pin down a single meaning, and confusing them causes genuine trouble in law, engineering and translation. There are three distinct phenomena, and they call for three distinct responses.

Ambiguity is the case where an expression has two or more discrete meanings. Lexical ambiguity involves a single word form: "bank" as a financial institution and as a river edge, "bat" as an animal and as a club. These are homonyms, historically unrelated words that collided in form. Structural ambiguity involves the arrangement of words: "visiting relatives can be tiresome" is ambiguous because "visiting" can be a participle modifying relatives or a gerund naming an activity. Scope ambiguity involves the relative order of logical operators, as in "Everyone loves someone", which either says each person has a beloved or that one person is universally loved. The remedy for ambiguity is disambiguation: context usually resolves it, and where stakes are high, drafting conventions force it. Legal drafters break "and/or" apart precisely because it is ambiguous between inclusive and exclusive readings.

Vagueness is different in kind. A vague term has one meaning but no sharp boundary of application. "Tall", "bald", "heap", "reasonable" and "soon" admit borderline cases where competent speakers who agree on all the facts still disagree on the verdict. Vagueness generates the sorites paradox, known since Eubulides of Miletus in the fourth century BCE: one grain of sand is not a heap, adding one grain to a non-heap never makes a heap, therefore no number of grains makes a heap. The premises look true and the conclusion is absurd. Responses include epistemicism, which says there is a sharp boundary we cannot know; supervaluationism, which says a sentence is true if true on every admissible way of sharpening the term; and degree theories, which assign truth values between 0 and 1. None is universally accepted. Crucially, vagueness is not a defect to be edited out; "reasonable care" is deliberately vague in negligence law so that a standard can adapt to circumstances a drafter could not foresee.

Polysemy is the third case: one word with several related senses radiating from a core. "Mouth" applies to a face, a river and a cave; "run" has dozens of senses covering athletes, machines, colours, noses, roads and elections; the Oxford English Dictionary lists more than four hundred for "set". Unlike homonymy, polysemy is systematic and productive, and often follows regular patterns such as container for contents ("I drank the whole bottle"), producer for product ("I am reading Austen") or place for institution ("Downing Street announced"). These regularities are so reliable that a speaker can extend them to new cases and be understood immediately.

The practical rule of thumb is diagnostic. If you can list the readings, it is ambiguity. If you cannot draw the line, it is vagueness. If the readings shade into one another and share a discernible core, it is polysemy.

sections.heading: Quantification, Scope, and Binding
sections.body:
Quantifier words such as every, some, no, most, few, both and at least three are among the hardest working items in any language, and getting them right was the achievement that turned logic into a usable tool for semantics. Aristotle's syllogistic handled a few quantified patterns; it was Frege's Begriffsschrift of 1879 that gave a general treatment by introducing variables and binding, which is arguably the single most important technical innovation in the history of logic.

The key idea is that a quantifier does not name a thing. "Every dog barks" does not describe an object called Every Dog. Instead the quantifier expresses a relation between two sets: the set of dogs and the set of barkers. "Every A is B" says the A set is a subset of the B set. "Some A is B" says the two sets overlap. "No A is B" says they are disjoint. "Most A are B" says more than half the A set is in the B set, which notably cannot be expressed in standard first-order logic at all, a result that motivated the theory of generalised quantifiers developed by Jon Barwise and Robin Cooper in 1981.

Scope is where quantifiers become genuinely tricky. Consider "Every student read a book." On one reading each student read a possibly different book; on the other there is one particular book that all of them read. The words and the syntax are identical, and the difference lies in which quantifier takes wider scope. Written in logical notation, the readings are: for every student x, there exists a book y such that x read y; versus, there exists a book y such that for every student x, x read y. The second entails the first but not conversely. Scope ambiguity multiplies fast: with three quantifiers there can be up to six readings, and negation, modals and intensional verbs add more.

Binding is the mechanism that ties pronouns to quantifiers. In "Every farmer who owns a donkey feeds it", the pronoun "it" is not referring to any specific donkey; its interpretation covaries with the quantification. This particular example, known as the donkey sentence and discussed by the medieval logician Walter Burley, resisted analysis for centuries because the pronoun sits outside the syntactic scope of "a donkey" yet behaves as if bound by it. The solution came in the early 1980s with Discourse Representation Theory, developed independently by Hans Kamp and Irene Heim, which builds a running representation of discourse referents that persists across sentence boundaries.

A robust empirical finding is that quantifiers are conservative: the truth of "Q A are B" depends only on the A set and its overlap with B, never on Bs that are not A. No natural language appears to have a quantifier violating this, which is one of the strongest candidate universals in semantics and a real constraint on what a possible human language can be.

sections.heading: Tense, Aspect, and Modality: Locating a Situation in Time and Possibility
sections.body:
Sentences do not merely describe situations; they place them in time and in a space of possibilities. Three interacting systems do this work, and languages differ enormously in which they grammaticalise.

Tense locates a situation relative to a reference point, normally the moment of speaking. Hans Reichenbach's 1947 analysis remains the standard framework and uses three times: the speech time S, the event time E, and a reference time R from which the event is viewed. Simple past is E and R together, both before S. Present perfect is E before R, with R at S, which is why "I have lost my keys" implies present relevance while "I lost my keys" does not. Past perfect puts E before R before S: "By the time she arrived, he had left." This three-point system explains why "I have lost my keys yesterday" is ungrammatical in English while its equivalent is fine in German and French, whose perfects have drifted into general past tenses.

Aspect concerns the internal shape of a situation rather than its location. The core distinction is perfective versus imperfective: "She read the book" presents the event as a bounded whole, while "She was reading the book" presents it from inside, in progress. Cutting across grammatical aspect is lexical aspect, or Aktionsart, classified by Zeno Vendler in 1957 into four types. States (know, own, be tall) hold without change and resist the progressive; activities (run, swim, push a cart) go on without a built-in endpoint; accomplishments (build a house, walk to school) have duration plus an endpoint; achievements (notice, arrive, win) are instantaneous transitions. The classes are testable. "In an hour" fits accomplishments and achievements; "for an hour" fits states and activities. This is why "He built the house for an hour" is odd, and why "He was arriving" needs a special slow-motion interpretation.

Modality concerns necessity and possibility. English modals are systematically ambiguous between two flavours. Epistemic modality concerns what the evidence permits: "She must be home, her car is outside" is an inference, not an order. Deontic modality concerns permission and obligation: "You must be home by ten" is a rule. "Can", "may", "should" and "might" all show this split. The standard analysis, due largely to Angelika Kratzer from the late 1970s, treats a modal as quantifying over possible worlds restricted by a conversational background: epistemic "must" says the proposition holds in every world compatible with what is known; deontic "must" says it holds in every world where the rules are obeyed.

Many languages add evidentiality, grammatically marking how the speaker knows. Turkish, Quechua and Tariana require a speaker to indicate whether a report is witnessed, inferred or hearsay. In Tariana, spoken in the Amazon, omitting the marker is not merely rude but ungrammatical, and a speaker must choose among roughly five evidential suffixes on every past-tense statement.

sections.heading: The Border with Pragmatics: What Is Said and What Is Meant
sections.body:
A speaker who answers "Do you want dessert?" with "I have to be up at five" has said nothing about dessert and yet has clearly declined. The gap between sentence meaning and speaker meaning is the province of pragmatics, and mapping the border is one of the most consequential problems in the field, because misplacing it makes a semantic theory either bloated or empty.

The foundational work is by the philosopher H. P. Grice, whose 1967 William James Lectures introduced the notion of conversational implicature. Grice proposed that conversation is governed by a Cooperative Principle: make your contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose of the exchange. Under it sit four maxims. Quantity: be as informative as required, and no more. Quality: do not say what you believe false or lack evidence for. Relation: be relevant. Manner: be brief, orderly and avoid obscurity and ambiguity.

Implicatures arise when a hearer assumes the speaker is obeying the principle even while apparently breaking a maxim. If a professor's entire reference letter reads "Mr Jones's handwriting is excellent and he attended punctually", the writer has flouted Quantity, and the reader infers a negative assessment that was never stated. Scalar implicature is the most studied family. Saying "Some of the students passed" implicates that not all did, because a cooperative speaker who knew all passed would have said so. Crucially the implicature is not part of the literal meaning, which is why it can be cancelled without contradiction: "Some, in fact all, of the students passed" is perfectly coherent. Cancellability is the standard diagnostic separating implicature from entailment; you cannot say "She has three children, in fact none."

A second diagnostic is detachability and calculability. An implicature should be derivable from the literal content plus the maxims plus context, and should survive rewording that preserves literal content. A third is non-detachability from what is said in the relevant respect: the inference tracks the content, not the particular words.

Grice's programme has been developed in two main directions. Neo-Griceans such as Laurence Horn and Stephen Levinson tidy the maxims into a smaller set of competing principles. Relevance Theory, developed by Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson from 1986, replaces the whole apparatus with a single cognitive principle: hearers seek the interpretation yielding the greatest cognitive effect for the least processing effort, and stop at the first interpretation meeting expectations of relevance.

The border remains genuinely contested. Some inferences that look pragmatic appear to feed into the truth conditions of larger sentences, which they should not do if they were purely post-semantic. "If some of the students passed, the rest will retake it" seems to use the not-all inference inside the antecedent. This has driven a body of work on so-called embedded implicatures and on grammatical theories of scalar inference, and there is no settled consensus about where the line falls.

sections.heading: Presupposition, Projection, and the Dynamics of Discourse
sections.body:
Some information carried by a sentence is not asserted but taken for granted. "Have you stopped skipping breakfast?" takes for granted that you have been skipping breakfast; "My sister lives in Cardiff" takes for granted that I have a sister; "It was Jamal who broke the window" takes for granted that somebody broke it. Such background content is called presupposition, and it behaves quite differently from ordinary assertion.

The defining diagnostic is survival under negation. If you negate "My sister lives in Cardiff", producing "My sister does not live in Cardiff", the claim about residence flips but the existence of the sister remains. The same holds under questioning, under modals and in the antecedent of a conditional. Because the presupposition escapes these embedding contexts, the phenomenon is often called projection. Constructions that trigger presuppositions include definite descriptions, factive verbs like know, realise and regret, change-of-state verbs like stop, start and continue, iteratives like again and another, cleft sentences, and focus particles like only and even.

Projection is not automatic, and predicting exactly when it is blocked is known as the projection problem, posed sharply by Lauri Karttunen in the 1970s. Certain environments filter presuppositions out. "If Ali has a sister, his sister lives in Cardiff" does not presuppose that Ali has a sister, because the antecedent already supplies it. "Either there is no King of France, or the King of France is in hiding" is fine for the same reason. Speakers can also accommodate: if you assert "I have to pick up my sister" to someone who did not know you had one, the hearer quietly adds the fact to the common ground rather than objecting. Robert Stalnaker's work from the 1970s onward made common ground the central notion, treating a conversation as a shared body of assumptions that assertions progressively narrow.

This led to a genuine shift in how meaning itself is modelled. Static truth-conditional semantics treats a sentence meaning as a set of worlds. Dynamic semantics, developed by Irene Heim in her 1982 dissertation and by Jeroen Groenendijk and Martin Stokhof in the 1990s, treats a sentence meaning as a function from one information state to another: meaning is context change potential. On this view a presupposition is a definedness condition, an input the update function requires in order to apply at all, which explains projection directly rather than by stipulation.

The dynamic view also solves problems that defeated static approaches. Anaphora across sentence boundaries becomes straightforward: "A man walked in. He sat down." introduces a discourse referent in the first sentence that the second picks up, without the pronoun needing to be inside any quantifier's syntactic scope. The same machinery handles modal subordination, as in "A wolf might come in. It would eat you first", where the pronoun depends on a merely possible wolf. Meaning becomes something a conversation builds incrementally rather than something a sentence has in isolation.

sections.heading: Thematic Roles, Argument Structure and Events
sections.body:
A verb does more than name an action; it specifies how many participants a situation has and what part each plays. These parts are thematic roles, sometimes called theta roles or semantic roles, and they are what allows a hearer to know who did what to whom independent of word order.

The commonly recognised roles form a short list. An Agent is a volitional instigator: the person in "Sam opened the door." A Patient or Theme is the entity affected or moved: the door. An Experiencer undergoes a mental state: "Sam feared the dog." A Goal is an endpoint, a Source an origin, a Location a place, an Instrument a means, and a Beneficiary the party the action is done for. Crucially the roles are not read off the grammar. In "The door opened", the door is subject but still Patient; in "The key opened the door", the subject is Instrument. Passive voice reverses the mapping without changing the roles: "The door was opened by Sam" assigns exactly the same roles as the active.

The mapping between roles and grammatical positions follows regular hierarchies. Cross-linguistically, if a clause has an Agent it is overwhelmingly likely to be the subject; if it has no Agent, an Experiencer or Instrument or Theme takes the slot. This ranking, Agent above Experiencer above Instrument above Theme above Location, is one of the most robust generalisations in the field, though the roles themselves are notoriously hard to define sharply, and David Dowty argued influentially in 1991 that they are better treated as clusters of proto-properties, so that a participant counts as Proto-Agent to the extent it is volitional, sentient, causally responsible and independently moving.

A parallel development treats verbs as describing events, following Donald Davidson's 1967 paper "The Logical Form of Action Sentences". Davidson noticed that "Jones buttered the toast in the bathroom with a knife at midnight" entails "Jones buttered the toast", and that this simple entailment is hard to derive if the verb is analysed as a predicate whose number of arguments changes with each modifier. His solution was to posit an event variable: there exists an event e such that e is a buttering, its agent is Jones, its theme is the toast, its location is the bathroom, its instrument is a knife and its time is midnight. Dropping conjuncts then yields the entailments automatically. This neo-Davidsonian format, in which every role is a separate two-place relation to the event, is now the standard representation in both linguistics and computational semantics.

The practical value shows in resources such as PropBank and FrameNet, which annotate corpora with role structure and drive semantic role labelling in machine systems. Knowing that "Sam sold Ben the bike" and "Ben bought the bike from Sam" describe one event with the same participants in different grammatical clothing is precisely the sort of inference that word-matching alone cannot reach.

sections.heading: Prototypes, Frames, and Cognitive Semantics
sections.body:
The formal tradition treats a category as a set with membership conditions. A different tradition, grounded in psychological experiment, argues that human categories do not work that way at all, and that any theory of meaning ignoring this is describing logic rather than language.

The decisive evidence came from Eleanor Rosch's experiments in the 1970s. Asked to rate how good an example of the category BIRD various species were, English speakers reliably placed robins and sparrows at the top, chickens and ostriches lower, and penguins near the bottom. Reaction times matched: subjects verified "a robin is a bird" faster than "a penguin is a bird", by margins of the order of a hundred milliseconds. Children acquire central members earlier. Speakers produce them first in listing tasks. On a classical set-membership account, all these should be equal, since all are equally birds. Rosch concluded that categories are organised around prototypes, best examples, with membership graded by similarity.

Rosch also identified a basic level in taxonomies at which categorisation is most efficient. Between the superordinate FURNITURE and the subordinate KITCHEN CHAIR sits CHAIR, and the basic level is where people have the shortest word, the fastest naming, the richest set of shared features, and a common motor interaction. Children learn basic-level terms first, and folk taxonomies across cultures converge on the same level, which is roughly the genus in biological classification.

Charles Fillmore's frame semantics, developed from the mid-1970s, adds a further insight: understanding a word often requires understanding a whole background scenario. You cannot know what "Tuesday" means without the seven-day week; you cannot know "bachelor" without a background of conventional marriage practice, which is why it feels wrong to call the Pope a bachelor even though he satisfies the feature analysis exactly. "Buy", "sell", "cost", "price", "goods" and "charge" all evoke a single commercial transaction frame and differ only in which participants they foreground. FrameNet, the Berkeley project Fillmore founded in 1997, has catalogued more than 1,200 such frames with tens of thousands of annotated example sentences.

The cognitive tradition also emphasises construal: two expressions can describe the same objective situation while imposing different perspectives. "The glass is half full" and "The glass is half empty" are truth-conditionally equivalent and pragmatically worlds apart. "The road runs through the valley" attributes motion to something stationary, a fictive-motion construction that Leonard Talmy showed is systematic across languages and correlates with measurable differences in how people mentally simulate the scene.

How far this displaces formal semantics is genuinely disputed. Prototype effects are real and replicated, but they may reflect how people access and apply categories rather than what those categories are. The word "bird" plausibly still denotes the set of birds even though penguins are odd ones, in the same way that odd numbers have graded typicality ratings while remaining a perfectly crisp mathematical set. The honest position is that formal and cognitive semantics measure different things, and the field has not agreed on how to combine them.

sections.heading: Metaphor, Metonymy and Figurative Meaning
sections.body:
Figurative language was long treated as decoration, a deviation from literal meaning that rhetoric could catalogue and semantics could ignore. That view collapsed under the weight of the evidence. Conservative estimates from corpus work put metaphorical expressions at roughly one word in every fifteen to twenty of ordinary written English, and much of it passes unnoticed precisely because it is conventional.

George Lakoff and Mark Johnson's Metaphors We Live By, published in 1980, made the central argument: metaphor is not primarily linguistic but conceptual. We do not merely say metaphorical things about argument; we think about argument in terms of war. The evidence is the systematic clustering of expressions. Your claims are indefensible. He attacked every weak point. I demolished his argument. Her criticisms were right on target. These are not independent turns of phrase but surface reflexes of a single mapping, ARGUMENT IS WAR, which projects structure from a concrete source domain onto an abstract target domain.

Other mappings are equally productive. TIME IS MONEY gives spend, waste, save, budget, invest and running out of time. UNDERSTANDING IS SEEING gives I see, that is clear, a murky explanation, shed light on, a brilliant insight. MORE IS UP gives prices rising, spirits soaring, output plummeting. Some mappings appear near-universal because they are grounded in bodily experience: affection is warmth, difficulty is weight, importance is size. Others are culturally specific, and translating them is where machine translation still visibly stumbles.

Metonymy is a distinct mechanism often confused with metaphor. Metaphor maps across domains on the basis of similarity; metonymy substitutes within a domain on the basis of contiguity or association. "The ham sandwich wants his bill" uses an order for a customer. "The White House denied it" uses a building for an administration. "We need more hands" uses a part for a whole, which is the special case called synecdoche. Metonymy is extraordinarily productive and largely invisible: "I am parked out back", "Shakespeare is on the top shelf", "the kettle is boiling".

How figurative meaning is processed is an empirical question with a shifting answer. The older standard-pragmatic model held that hearers compute the literal meaning, detect its absurdity, then search for a figurative interpretation. Reaction-time studies from Sam Glucksberg and others in the 1980s and 1990s undercut this: familiar metaphors are understood as fast as literal paraphrases, with no measurable extra cost, which suggests conventional metaphor is accessed directly rather than repaired. Novel metaphor does show processing cost, so the truth appears to be that conventionality, not figurativeness, is what determines effort. The practical consequence is that a dictionary listing only literal senses is describing a small and unrepresentative fraction of how the words are actually used.

sections.heading: The Formal Toolkit: Types, Functions and a Worked Derivation
sections.body:
Formal semantics needs a way to say precisely how the meaning of a whole is computed from the meanings of the parts. The standard tool is a typed lambda calculus, introduced to linguistics by Richard Montague and now taught in every graduate semantics course. The apparatus looks forbidding and is actually simple: everything is either an entity, a truth value, or a function built from those two.

Two basic types are assumed. Type e is the type of entities, individuals in the domain. Type t is the type of truth values, true or false. From these, complex types are built by a single rule: if a and b are types, then the type of functions from a-things to b-things, written a to b, is also a type. An intransitive verb such as "sleeps" takes an entity and returns a truth value, so its type is e to t. A transitive verb such as "loves" takes an entity and returns something of type e to t, so its type is e to (e to t). An adjective in predicative position is e to t. A determiner such as "every" takes a noun meaning of type e to t and returns a quantifier, giving the type (e to t) to ((e to t) to t).

Lambda notation writes such functions explicitly. The meaning of "sleeps" is written as: lambda x, sleep(x), read as the function that takes an entity x and returns true if x sleeps. Combination is then function application, and there is only one combinatorial rule to learn. Applying lambda x, sleep(x) to the individual Mary yields sleep(Mary), a truth value. This step is called beta reduction and simply consists of substituting the argument for the variable and deleting the lambda.

A worked derivation makes the machinery concrete. Take "Mary loves John." The meaning of "loves" is lambda y, lambda x, love(x, y): a function that first takes the object, then the subject. Syntax combines the verb with its object first, so applying it to John gives lambda x, love(x, John). That result is now of type e to t, exactly the type of an intransitive verb phrase, which is a satisfying confirmation that the type system tracks the grammar. Combining that with the subject Mary yields love(Mary, John), of type t. The sentence is true if and only if Mary stands in the loving relation to John.

Quantifiers require one extra idea, type-lifting, because "every student" cannot simply be an entity. Its meaning is lambda P, for all x, student(x) implies P(x): a function taking a property and returning a truth value. Applying it to the property lambda x, love(x, John) gives: for all x, student(x) implies love(x, John). The whole apparatus is thus two types, one combination rule and one reduction step, and from that base the entire truth-conditional treatment of English is assembled.

sections.heading: Meaning Across Languages: Universals and Relativity
sections.body:
Comparing how different languages encode meaning is the sharpest available test of which semantic structures are human and which are local convention. The results are more nuanced than either universalist or relativist slogans suggest.

Colour is the classic case study. Brent Berlin and Paul Kay's 1969 survey of ninety-eight languages found that basic colour terms are not distributed arbitrarily. Languages with only two terms divide light-warm from dark-cool. A third term is always red. The fourth and fifth are green and yellow in either order, the sixth blue, the seventh brown, and then purple, pink, orange and grey in no fixed order. Later work, including the World Color Survey covering 110 unwritten languages, softened the claims: the sequence is a strong statistical tendency rather than a law, and focal colours cluster more tightly than boundaries do. Still, the pattern is not what pure convention would predict, and it plausibly reflects the physiology of the visual system.

Spatial language runs the other way. English uses a relative frame of reference, describing a cup as to the left of a plate, which flips when you walk round the table. Guugu Yimithirr, spoken in northern Queensland, uses absolute cardinal directions for everything, so the cup is north of the plate whether you move or not, and speakers maintain accurate dead reckoning even inside unfamiliar buildings. Stephen Levinson's group at Nijmegen showed in the 1990s that this correlates with non-linguistic spatial memory: absolute-frame speakers reconstruct arrays in absolute terms, relative-frame speakers in relative terms. That is a genuine cognitive difference tracking a linguistic one.

Other well-attested differences include grammatical number, where Pirahã appears to lack exact number words above roughly two, with corresponding difficulty in exact large-quantity matching tasks; motion encoding, where Talmy's typology separates verb-framed languages such as Spanish, which encode path in the verb and manner in a modifier, from satellite-framed languages such as English, which do the reverse, so that "she ran into the room" naturally becomes "entró corriendo"; and evidentiality, which some languages require and English merely permits.

The honest summary of the linguistic relativity debate is deflationary but not dismissive. The strong Sapir-Whorf claim, that language determines thought and makes some concepts unthinkable, has no serious empirical support; people readily learn distinctions their language does not encode. The weak claim, that habitual linguistic categories bias attention, memory and judgment in measurable ways, has substantial support with effect sizes that are real but modest and often disappear under verbal interference, which suggests language is being used as a thinking tool rather than constraining thought at its foundations.

For a translator the practical lesson is concrete. There is usually no word-to-word mapping. German Schadenfreude, Portuguese saudade, Japanese amae and Russian toska are famous because they package feelings English distributes across phrases. Translation succeeds by reconstructing the whole situation described, which is exactly what frame semantics predicts it must do.

sections.heading: Distributional and Computational Semantics
sections.body:
The most consequential development in applied semantics of the last two decades came not from linguistics or philosophy but from statistics. The distributional hypothesis holds that words appearing in similar contexts have similar meanings. Zellig Harris stated it in 1954 and J. R. Firth gave it the memorable formulation in 1957; computing power finally made it usable around 2013.

The method is straightforward in outline. Take a very large text corpus. Represent each word by a vector of numbers derived from the words it co-occurs with. Words used similarly end up with similar vectors, measured by the cosine of the angle between them. Early versions built enormous sparse count matrices and reduced them with linear algebra, a technique called Latent Semantic Analysis introduced in 1988. The 2013 word2vec models of Tomas Mikolov's group learned dense vectors of typically 100 to 300 dimensions by training a small neural network to predict a word from its neighbours, and the resulting spaces showed striking arithmetic regularities: the vector for king minus man plus woman lands near queen; Paris minus France plus Italy lands near Rome.

The critical limitation of those early embeddings was that each word type got one vector, so "bank" was a blur of the financial and riverside senses. Contextual models, beginning with ELMo and then BERT in 2018 and the large transformer language models that followed, fixed this by producing a different vector for each occurrence, computed from the whole surrounding sentence. Word sense disambiguation, a task that had resisted decades of hand-built effort, became largely solved as a by-product.

What these systems capture and what they miss is a live and serious question. They plainly capture a great deal of lexical relatedness, selectional preference, register and topical association, and they support fluent generation. They are much weaker on exactly the phenomena the formal tradition was built for: negation, quantifier scope, systematic compositional entailment and reliable reference tracking. A model may treat "the cat is on the mat" and "the cat is not on the mat" as highly similar, because they share almost all their context, when they are in fact contradictory. Whether scale alone closes this gap is contested and should not be asserted confidently in either direction.

The practical middle ground is hybrid. Retrieval and search benefit from distributional similarity; legal, medical and safety-critical inference still benefits from explicit structured representation with checkable logic. Formal resources built by hand, including WordNet, FrameNet, PropBank and the various description-logic ontologies underlying the Semantic Web, remain in production use precisely because their inferences are auditable. A vector space can tell you two documents are similar; it cannot show its work. For a semanticist, the deepest interest of these systems is empirical: they are large-scale evidence about how much of meaning is recoverable from distribution alone, and the answer, surprising to almost everyone in 1990, is a great deal but not all.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and Repair: Where Meaning Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Semantic analysis is not only academic. Lawyers, technical writers, standards committees and engineers all do applied semantics, usually without the vocabulary, and a handful of concrete techniques transfer directly from the theory to the desk.

The first technique is entailment testing. To check whether a sentence says what you intend, ask what must be true if it is true, and what would still be true if you negated it. If a proposition survives negation, you have written a presupposition rather than a claim, and presuppositions are precisely what readers absorb without noticing and later dispute. A questionnaire item reading "How satisfied were you with the improved service?" presupposes improvement and will bias every response.

The second is scope discipline. Whenever a sentence contains two or more of quantifiers, negation, modals or conditionals, enumerate the readings explicitly. "All employees may not park here" has a prohibition reading and a partial-permission reading, and both have appeared in real signage. Rewriting as "No employee may park here" or "Some employees may not park here" eliminates the problem. The Australian and British legislative drafting offices maintain internal manuals built almost entirely from this observation.

The third is controlled vocabulary. Where precision matters, fix a defined term and use only that term, even where repetition is stylistically ugly. Elegant variation is a semantic hazard: if a contract uses "the goods", "the products" and "the items", a reader is entitled to infer three referents, because a competent speaker who meant one thing would have used one word. This is Grice's Manner maxim doing unwanted work.
steps: Write the sentence, then state in one line what it commits you to. If you cannot, the sentence is not yet finished.
Negate the whole sentence and list what still survives. Anything surviving is presupposed, not asserted; decide deliberately whether you want it there.

Circle every quantifier (all, each, any, some, no, most), every negation, every modal (may, must, shall, can) and every conditional. If two or more appear, write out each possible reading in plain words and pick one.
Replace every pronoun with the full noun phrase it refers to. If more than one antecedent is grammatically available, the pronoun is unsafe even if the intended reading is obvious to you.
Check every vague term (reasonable, promptly, material, substantial, adequate). Either give it a number, or record deliberately that you want the flexibility and accept the litigation risk.
Give the draft to a reader with no context and ask them to paraphrase it. Divergence between their paraphrase and your intent locates the defect precisely.
For lists, state whether they are exhaustive or illustrative. 'Including' is ambiguous between the two; 'including without limitation' and 'consisting only of' are not.

guides.title: Pragmatics — Meaning in Context
guides.summary: A full account of pragmatics: how listeners recover what a speaker means beyond what the words literally say, covering deixis, implicature, speech acts, presupposition, politeness, relevance, and how pragmatic ability develops, varies across cultures, and breaks down.

sections.heading: What Pragmatics Is and Why It Matters
sections.body:
Pragmatics is the study of how people work out what someone means, as opposed to what their words strictly say. If a friend standing by a shut window says "It's freezing in here," the sentence describes a temperature, but almost nobody hears it as a weather report. It is a request to close the window, or a complaint, or an apology for the state of the flat, depending on who is speaking and to whom. The gap between the encoded sentence and the message actually delivered is the whole subject matter of pragmatics. Semantics, its sister field, asks what a sentence means in the abstract — the contribution the words and grammar make no matter who utters them. Pragmatics asks what a speaker means by uttering that sentence here, now, to this person, given everything both parties already know.

The gap is not a marginal quirk of language. It is enormous and constant. Linguists estimate that a very large fraction of the information transmitted in ordinary conversation is never encoded in the words at all; it is inferred. Consider "Some of the students passed." The words are compatible with all of them passing — "some" in logic means "at least one" — yet listeners reliably conclude that not all did. Consider "Can you pass the salt?" which is grammatically a question about ability and is answered with an action, not with "yes." Consider "I've had breakfast," which normally means today, not once in a lifetime, though nothing in the sentence says so. Each of these inferences is automatic, fast, and defeasible: the speaker can cancel it without contradicting themselves, as in "Some, in fact all, of the students passed."

Pragmatics matters practically because misfires are expensive. Contract disputes, diplomatic incidents, medical errors, and everyday domestic rows very often turn on a difference between what was said and what was taken. It matters for anyone learning a second language, because a speaker can have flawless grammar and still be rude, because the pragmatic conventions of directness and deference differ enormously across communities. It matters in clinical settings, because several conditions — autism, right-hemisphere brain damage, schizophrenia, some dementias — leave the grammar intact while impairing the inferential machinery. And it matters for machines: a system that parses syntax perfectly but cannot infer that "I'm looking for a good Thai place" is a request rather than an autobiographical statement is not usable.

The field's modern shape was set in the mid-twentieth century by philosophers rather than linguists. Charles Morris in 1938 first divided the study of signs into syntax, semantics and pragmatics, defining pragmatics as the relation of signs to their interpreters. J. L. Austin's lectures at Harvard in 1955, published posthumously in 1962 as How to Do Things with Words, established that saying is doing. H. P. Grice's William James Lectures at Harvard in 1967 gave the field its central engine, a theory of how cooperative reasoning generates inference. Everything since has been elaboration, revision, or reaction to those foundations.

sections.heading: Sentence Meaning, Speaker Meaning and the Semantics Boundary
sections.body:
The distinction that organises the whole field is between what a sentence means and what a speaker means by it on an occasion. Sentence meaning is stable, conventional and learnable from a dictionary and a grammar. Speaker meaning is occasion-specific and depends on intentions. Grice defined speaker meaning intentionally and recursively in a 1957 paper: a speaker means something by an utterance if they intend it to produce an effect in the hearer, and intend that effect to be produced partly by the hearer's recognition of that very intention. The recursion matters. If I leave a bloodstained glove at a crime scene to make you believe someone is guilty, I intend an effect, but I do not want you to recognise my intention — so I have not meant anything in the communicative sense. Communication is overt in a way that manipulation is not.

Between pure sentence meaning and full speaker meaning sits a contested middle layer. Take "She didn't take it." The grammar and dictionary alone do not tell you who "she" is, what "it" is, or when this happened. Filling these in is called saturation, and the result is usually labelled "what is said" — the proposition the speaker explicitly expressed. Only above that layer do we place implicature, the things communicated without being said. The trouble is that many enrichments look intermediate. "It'll take time" plainly means it will take a considerable amount of time, but nothing forces that reading grammatically. "He drank the bottle" means the contents. "I have nothing to wear" means nothing appropriate for the occasion.

Two schools disagree about where to file such cases. Literalists, following Grice fairly closely, want "what is said" to stay close to the linguistic form and push enrichment into implicature. Contextualists, including relevance theorists and philosophers like François Recanati, argue that pragmatic processes intrude into the proposition expressed itself — a position sometimes called "pragmatic intrusion" or "free enrichment." The debate is genuinely unresolved and it is worth being honest about that. It matters for how one analyses courtroom testimony, where the difference between lying and merely misleading depends on whether a misleading enrichment counts as part of what was asserted.

A related boundary case is ambiguity resolution. "The bank was steep" versus "The bank was closed" are disambiguated by context, but nobody thinks the speaker implied anything; they simply selected a lexical entry. Most analysts count disambiguation and reference assignment as pre-semantic pragmatic processes: pragmatic in that they use context, but feeding into what is said rather than adding to it.

A practical test for separating layers is cancellability. Genuine implicatures can be withdrawn without self-contradiction — "Some passed; in fact all did" is fine. What is said cannot be withdrawn that way — "The cat is on the mat, but no cat is on any mat" is contradictory. Cancellability is not a perfect diagnostic, since some implicatures resist cancellation in specific contexts, but it remains the first tool a working analyst reaches for.

sections.heading: Deixis: Language Anchored to the Speech Situation
sections.body:
Some expressions cannot be interpreted at all without knowing who spoke, where, and when. These are deictic, from the Greek for pointing. A note reading "Meet me here tomorrow" found on a park bench is essentially useless: it has perfect grammar and no determinable content. The classic categories are person deixis (I, you, we, they), place deixis (here, there, this, that, come, go, bring, take), and time deixis (now, then, today, yesterday, next week, and crucially all tense marking). Two further categories are commonly added: discourse deixis, which points to parts of the unfolding text ("as I said above," "the following argument"), and social deixis, which encodes relationships between participants.

The anchor point is called the deictic centre: canonically the speaker, at the speaker's location, at the moment of speaking. Most deictic interpretation is relative to that centre. "Come here" invites motion toward the speaker; "go there" is motion away. But centres shift. Written notes project into the reader's time — "I am not here now" on an answering machine is coherent only because the recording projects the deictic centre forward to playback. Narrators shift the centre into a character's viewpoint, which is what produces free indirect style: "Tomorrow would be different, she thought" mixes the narrator's past tense with the character's future-oriented "tomorrow."

Languages carve deictic space very differently. English has a two-term spatial system, this/that. Spanish has three: este (near speaker), ese (near hearer), aquel (far from both). Japanese similarly uses ko-, so-, a-. Some languages, notably Guugu Yimithirr in north Queensland, encode direction absolutely rather than relatively: speakers say the equivalent of "there is an ant on your south leg," and are documented to maintain accurate dead-reckoning of compass direction from early childhood. This is one of the strongest surviving pieces of evidence for a genuine, if bounded, linguistic influence on habitual cognition.

Social deixis is elaborately grammaticalised in many languages. The T/V distinction — French tu/vous, German du/Sie, Russian ty/vy, Spanish tú/usted — forces every speaker to encode a social relationship in every second-person reference. There is no neutral option; silence is not available. Brown and Gilman's classic 1960 study traced how the choice historically shifted from marking power asymmetry to marking solidarity. Japanese and Korean go far further, with honorific verb morphology, humbling forms for one's own actions, and referent honorifics keyed to the person spoken about rather than spoken to.

Deixis is where pragmatics is least deniable. Even the strictest semanticist concedes that the content of "I" depends on who says it. That concession is the wedge that opens the rest of the field: once context is admitted for pronouns, there is no principled way to exclude it elsewhere.

sections.heading: Grice's Cooperative Principle and the Conversational Maxims
sections.body:
H. P. Grice proposed that conversation is a rational, cooperative activity, and that participants tacitly assume this. His Cooperative Principle instructs: make your contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged. Under it he grouped four categories of maxim, named after Kant's categories.

Quantity has two parts: make your contribution as informative as required, and do not make it more informative than required. Quality also has two: do not say what you believe to be false, and do not say that for which you lack adequate evidence. Relation has one: be relevant. Manner covers the how rather than the what: avoid obscurity of expression, avoid ambiguity, be brief, and be orderly.

The crucial and frequently misunderstood point is that these are not rules of etiquette and not instructions Grice thought people obey. They are descriptions of the assumptions hearers make, and their real work is done when they appear to be broken. If a colleague asks how a job candidate performed and the referee writes only "Her handwriting is excellent and she was always punctual," the referee has said nothing false. But the answer is grossly under-informative for the purpose, and the reader, assuming the referee is nonetheless cooperating at a deeper level, infers the missing verdict: the candidate is poor. Grice called this exploitation or flouting — the maxim is breached at the level of what is said in order to communicate something at the level of what is meant.

Grice distinguished several ways a maxim can fail to be met. A speaker may quietly violate one, as in a lie, in which case no implicature arises because the hearer is deceived. A speaker may opt out — "I cannot say more, I'm bound by confidentiality" — which blocks inference explicitly. A speaker may face a clash, unable to satisfy Quantity without violating Quality, and the hedge that results ("I think it's somewhere in Berkshire") implicates uncertainty. And a speaker may flout, blatantly and visibly breaching a maxim while remaining evidently cooperative, which is the engine of irony, metaphor, hyperbole and understatement.

Grice's system is elegant but has been substantially criticised. The maxims overlap: brevity under Manner does much of the work of Quantity. They are of uneven status, since Quality seems to have a special foundational role — without a presumption of truthfulness the others cannot function. Their number is arbitrary; Grice himself said others might be added. Laurence Horn reduced them to two opposed principles, Q ("say enough") and R ("don't say too much"), whose tension explains a great deal of the pattern. Stephen Levinson proposed three heuristics, Q, I and M. Relevance theorists reduced them to one. Nonetheless the maxims survive as a working vocabulary because they are teachable and because they carve up recognisable phenomena. Almost every subsequent theory can be read as an attempt to derive them from something more basic.

sections.heading: Implicature: Generalised, Particularised, and Conventional
sections.body:
An implicature is something communicated without being said. Grice divided them into conversational, which arise from the Cooperative Principle plus context, and conventional, which are attached to particular words regardless of context.

Conversational implicatures split further. Particularised implicatures depend heavily on the specific situation. If A asks "Are you coming to the party?" and B answers "I have to work," the inference that B is not coming depends on knowing that working and partying conflict here. Change the context — the party is at B's workplace — and the implicature vanishes. Generalised implicatures ride along with particular forms in nearly all contexts. "Some of the guests left" normally implicates that not all did. "I broke a finger yesterday" normally implicates it was my own, since a possessive would otherwise have been used. "He walked into a house" implicates it was not his own house.

The best-studied generalised case is scalar implicature. Words fall on informational scales ordered by strength: <all, most, many, some>, <and, or>, <always, often, sometimes>, <certain, probable, possible>, <hot, warm>. Uttering a weaker term implicates that the speaker was not in a position to assert the stronger, by Quantity: if all had passed, "all" was available, shorter and more informative, so the choice of "some" signals its unavailability. This is sometimes formalised as the epistemic step: the hearer first infers that the speaker does not know the stronger claim to be true, and then, assuming the speaker is well-informed, strengthens this to the speaker knowing it to be false.

Scalar implicature has become a major experimental battleground because it lets researchers test processing costs. Reading-time and eye-tracking studies through the 2000s, notably by Ira Noveck, Anne Bott and Lewis, generally found that computing the implicature-enriched reading takes measurable extra time, on the order of tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds, supporting a view where enrichment is an effortful pragmatic addition. Other studies, using different tasks and richer contexts, find little or no cost, supporting a more grammatical or default view. The honest summary is that the cost depends heavily on task and context, and the theoretical dispute is live.

Conventional implicatures are different in kind. In "He is poor but honest," the word "but" contributes a sense of contrast. That contrast is not part of the truth conditions — the sentence is true whenever he is poor and honest, contrast or not — but neither is it calculable from context. It is simply attached to "but." Similar items include "even," "yet," "therefore," "moreover," and in some analyses appositives and expressives like "that idiot Smith." Conventional implicatures are not cancellable and not calculable, which is exactly why they sit awkwardly in Grice's system; some later theorists dissolve the category into a separate dimension of meaning, following Chris Potts's work on conventional implicature and expressives in 2005.

sections.heading: Testing for Implicature: A Working Procedure
sections.body:
Deciding whether a piece of communicated content is an implicature, part of what is said, a presupposition, or an entailment is the central analytic task in the field, and it is done with a small set of diagnostics applied in order. The procedure below is what a linguist actually runs when confronted with a disputed example.

The diagnostics are not individually decisive. What gives confidence is convergence: when four or five tests agree, the classification is secure. When they conflict, that conflict usually marks a case at a theoretical boundary.
steps: State the utterance and the disputed inference precisely. Write out the sentence and the candidate inference as separate propositions. Vagueness at this stage produces hours of wasted argument. For example: utterance 'Some of the eggs are cracked'; candidate inference 'Not all of the eggs are cracked'.

Apply the cancellability test. Append a clause denying the inference and check for contradiction. 'Some of the eggs are cracked — in fact all of them are' is coherent, so the inference is defeasible and is a strong candidate for conversational implicature. By contrast 'Some of the eggs are cracked, but no eggs are cracked' is contradictory, showing that the existential content is entailed, not implicated.

Apply the reinforceability test. Restate the inference explicitly and check for redundancy. 'Some but not all of the eggs are cracked' sounds natural rather than tautological, which supports implicature status. Entailments, by contrast, sound absurdly redundant when reinforced: 'She is a bachelor and unmarried' feels wrong.

Apply the detachability test. Substitute a truth-conditionally equivalent expression and see whether the inference survives. Conversational implicatures are non-detachable, because they arise from what was said rather than how it was worded: 'a few of the eggs are cracked' carries the same not-all inference. Conventional implicatures are detachable: replacing 'but' with 'and' removes the contrast, so contrast is conventional.

Apply the projection test for presupposition. Embed the sentence under negation, in a question, and in a conditional antecedent. Presuppositions survive all three: 'The king of France is not bald' and 'Is the king of France bald?' both still presuppose a French king exists. Implicatures generally do not survive negation this way.

Check calculability. Try to derive the inference step by step from what was said plus the Cooperative Principle plus mutually known background. If you can write the derivation out — the speaker said the weaker term, the stronger was available, they are cooperative and informed, therefore the stronger is false — the inference is conversational. If no such derivation exists and the meaning simply attaches to a word, it is conventional.

Check context-dependence to sort generalised from particularised. Transplant the utterance into three or four unrelated contexts. If the inference recurs everywhere, it is generalised; if it evaporates when the background changes, it is particularised.

Record the residue honestly. If tests conflict — the inference is cancellable but also detachable, say — do not force a verdict. Note the conflict, name the competing analyses, and treat the example as evidence bearing on the theoretical dispute rather than as a solved case.

sections.heading: Speech Act Theory: Saying as Doing
sections.body:
J. L. Austin's starting observation was that some utterances do not describe the world but change it. Saying "I name this ship the Queen Elizabeth" while smashing a bottle against the bow does not report a naming; it performs one. "I bet you five pounds it rains," "I apologise," "I hereby resign," "I pronounce you married" — these he called performatives, contrasting them with constatives, which state facts and can be true or false. Performatives cannot be true or false; they can only succeed or fail, and Austin catalogued the conditions of success as felicity conditions.

Felicity conditions come in types. There must be an accepted conventional procedure with a conventional effect, invoked in appropriate circumstances by appropriate persons: a passerby cannot marry a couple, and a ship cannot be named by someone not authorised to name it. The procedure must be executed completely and correctly. And the participants must have the appropriate thoughts and intentions: promising while intending not to perform is an abuse, not a nullity — the promise exists but is insincere. Austin distinguished misfires, where the act fails to come off at all, from abuses, where it comes off but hollowly.

Austin then dismantled his own distinction. Stating, he argued, is itself an act — the act of asserting — with its own felicity conditions, and can be infelicitous in the same ways. This collapse produced his general theory: every utterance simultaneously performs three acts. The locutionary act is the act of producing a meaningful sentence with sense and reference. The illocutionary act is what is done in saying it — promising, warning, asking, ordering. The perlocutionary act is the effect brought about by saying it — persuading, frightening, convincing, annoying. Illocution is conventional and recoverable; perlocution is causal and not guaranteed. I can warn you (illocution) without alarming you (perlocution).

John Searle systematised the theory in 1969 and 1975, proposing that illocutionary acts fall into five classes. Assertives commit the speaker to the truth of a proposition (state, claim, report, conclude). Directives attempt to get the hearer to do something (request, order, beg, advise). Commissives commit the speaker to a future action (promise, offer, threaten, guarantee). Expressives convey a psychological state (thank, apologise, congratulate, condole). Declarations change reality by their utterance, given institutional authority (resign, appoint, excommunicate, declare war).

Searle also specified constitutive rules for each act. A promise requires a propositional content condition (a future act by the speaker), a preparatory condition (the hearer wants it done and it would not happen anyway), a sincerity condition (the speaker intends to do it), and an essential condition (the utterance counts as undertaking an obligation). These rules do more than classify; they explain why particular utterances feel odd. "I promise I broke the window" fails the content condition, which is why it can only be heard as an emphatic assertion rather than a promise.

sections.heading: Indirect Speech Acts and How Requests Get Made
sections.body:
Most requests in English are not issued as imperatives. "Shut the door" is grammatically the direct form, but people far more often say "Could you shut the door?", "Would you mind shutting the door?", "It's cold in here," or "The door's open." These are indirect speech acts: the utterance performs one illocutionary act by way of performing another. Searle's account is that the hearer recognises the literal act (a question about ability), notices that it would be pointless or uninformative as such, and derives the intended act by reasoning over the felicity conditions of requesting.

The reasoning is systematic. A request has preparatory conditions (the hearer is able to comply), sincerity conditions (the speaker wants it), content conditions (a future act by the hearer), and essential conditions. Indirect requests characteristically either question a preparatory condition ("Can you...?" "Do you have...?"), assert a sincerity condition ("I'd like you to..."), question a content condition ("Will you...?"), or state a reason ("It's stuffy in here"). Because the pattern is systematic, learners can be taught it explicitly.

Crucially, many of these forms have become conventionalised. "Can you pass the salt?" is not really computed afresh each time; it is a standardised form for requesting, which is why "Yes" alone is a joke rather than a cooperative answer, and why "please" can be inserted ("Can you please pass the salt?") even though "please" belongs to requests, not questions.
