This item-and-arrangement tradition descends from Bloomfield through post-war American structuralism and thrives today in Distributed Morphology, developed by Morris Halle and Alec Marantz from 1993, which abolishes a separate word-building module altogether: the same syntactic engine builds words and sentences, and phonological material is inserted late, spelling out feature bundles, with special rules handling irregulars as contextual spell-outs, so "went" is what the past-tense node sounds like in the context of GO. Word-based or realizational theories run the other way. They take the word or the lexeme as basic and treat morphology as rules relating whole words, or as functions from a lexeme plus a feature set to a form. The tradition runs from ancient word-and-paradigm grammar, the Greek and Latin schoolroom method of reciting amo, amas, amat, through Hockett's defense of it in 1954, to modern frameworks such as Gregory Stump's Paradigm Function Morphology in 2001 and Aronoff's insistence that some morphology is purely morphological, "morphomic," serving no syntactic or semantic master. The realizational camp points to phenomena morphemes handle badly: cumulative exponence, where one ending expresses five categories at once; extended exponence, where one category is marked in several places simultaneously, as in German ge-sung-en, where past participle is signaled by prefix, vowel change, and suffix together; syncretism, where distinct feature bundles systematically share a form; and defectiveness, paradigm holes like Russian's missing first-person singular of "to win," which speakers simply avoid. A third strand, Ray Jackendoff's and Jenny Audring's Relational Morphology in 2020 and Construction Morphology developed by Geert Booij from 2010, treats patterns as constructions: schemas like "X-ness means the property of being X" stored alongside their instantiations, with productivity as schema extension, a view that integrates smoothly with usage-based and frequency-sensitive psycholinguistics. Optimality Theory, imported from phonology in the 1990s, recast allomorph choice as constraint competition, and information-theoretic work by Farrell Ackerman and Robert Malouf in 2013 reframed paradigms as codes, proposing that languages keep the conditional entropy of predicting one cell of a paradigm from another low enough to be learnable, a testable quantitative universal. What genuinely divides the camps is the status of the morpheme: real mental atom or descriptive convenience. What unites them is larger than what divides: all agree words have layered structure, that regularity and irregularity coexist along a gradient, that frequency conditions storage, and that morphology interfaces intimately with phonology on one side and syntax on the other. A reader should treat the frameworks as instruments, not faiths: agglutinative Turkish flatters morpheme-based models, fusional Latin flatters realizational ones, and an honest theory must play both.

sections.heading: Computational Morphology: Machines That Parse Words
sections.body: Making computers analyze and generate words is one of language technology's oldest and most practical problems, and morphology is where many languages make or break a system. The foundational engineering insight, due to Kimmo Koskenniemi's 1983 two-level morphology and generalized in the finite-state calculus developed at Xerox by Ronald Kaplan, Martin Kay, Lauri Karttunen, and colleagues, is that most morphology, concatenation plus regular sound alternations, can be modeled by finite-state transducers: mathematically simple devices mapping surface forms like "flies" to analyses like "fly plus noun plural" and back again, running in both directions at high speed. Finite-state analyzers were built for Finnish, Turkish, Arabic, and hundreds of other languages, and they remain the backbone of spell checkers, where the dictionary for an agglutinative language cannot possibly list every word: a Turkish spell checker must accept forms like evlerimizdekilerden, "from the ones at our houses," which will never appear in any wordlist, and only a generative model of suffixation can do so. Simpler tools serve information retrieval: stemmers such as Martin Porter's 1980 algorithm strip suffixes heuristically so that a search for "connect" also matches "connected," "connection," and "connecting," accepting some overstemming errors, "university" and "universe" colliding, as the price of recall. Lemmatizers do the job properly, mapping each form to its dictionary headword using an analyzer and context. Morphology is also where machine translation historically stumbled: translating English into Finnish or Hungarian requires generating case endings English never expresses, and statistical systems of the 2000s produced fluent stems with wrong endings until factored and morphology-aware models intervened. The unsupervised discovery of morphology from raw text became a scientific benchmark: systems like Linguistica by John Goldsmith in 2001 and Morfessor from Helsinki in 2002 induce plausible segmentations by minimum description length, essentially rediscovering suffixes as compression, an approach with obvious interest for theories of child learning. The neural era changed the surface but not the problem. Modern large language models do not receive words at all; their tokenizers, using byte-pair encoding introduced for translation by Rico Sennrich in 2016, split text into frequent subword chunks, so "unbelievability" might arrive as "un," "believ," "abil," "ity." These chunks only loosely track true morphemes, and tokenization artifacts measurably hurt performance on rich morphologies, one reason benchmarks show weaker results for Turkish or Finnish than corpus size alone predicts, and why morphologically aware tokenization remains an active research area. Shared tasks such as the SIGMORPHON reinflection competitions, running since 2016, ask systems to produce, say, the third-person plural past of a novel verb across dozens of languages; neural sequence models now exceed 95 percent accuracy on many, yet still fail on the suppletion and rare-pattern cases that trouble human learners least, a revealing asymmetry. For low-resource and endangered languages, hand-built finite-state morphologies remain vital infrastructure, powering dictionaries, teaching tools, and text input, and often constitute the most complete scientific description of the language ever made.

sections.heading: How to Analyze Words: A Working Method
sections.body: Morphological analysis is a learnable craft, used by field linguists documenting undescribed languages, by students facing a problem set, and by anyone trying to decode an unfamiliar technical term. The method is comparative at its core: morphemes are discovered by contrast, never by staring at a single word. Given a data set, say Swahili ninasoma "I am reading," unasoma "you are reading," ninapika "I am cooking," the analyst aligns forms that differ minimally in meaning and form, and the differences isolate the morphemes: ni- "I," u- "you," -na- present, -soma "read," -pika "cook." Each hypothesis is then tested for consistency across the whole set, and residues, pieces left unexplained, are flagged rather than forced. Several disciplines keep the craft honest. First, gloss everything: the interlinear glossing conventions standardized as the Leipzig Glossing Rules in 2008 require each morpheme in the object language to sit above an aligned label, so analyses are explicit and checkable. Second, distinguish forms from spellings: analyze pronunciations, since orthography lags and lies; English "boxes" spells its plural -es but the morphology is the same z-family suffix as in "dogs." Third, respect allomorphy: before positing two morphemes, ask whether one morpheme with phonologically conditioned variants explains the data more economically. Fourth, beware accidental resemblance: the -er of "brother" is not the agentive -er of "baker," because "broth" plus agent yields nonsense; meaning must license every cut. The procedure below condenses field practice into a repeatable sequence for any language data.
steps: 1. Assemble a minimal data set: collect at least six to ten words or short forms with reliable meanings, ideally forming near-minimal pairs that differ in one grammatical feature at a time, such as singular versus plural or present versus past.
2. Transcribe phonetically, not orthographically, so that real sound alternations are visible and spelling conventions cannot mislead the segmentation.
3. Align and contrast: place forms with shared meaning components side by side, mark the recurring substrings, and propose a candidate cut wherever a constant form pairs with a constant meaning.
4. Extract a candidate morpheme inventory: list each proposed root and affix with its gloss, its position class such as prefix or suffix, and every attested allomorph.
5. Test every word in the set against the inventory: each form must be fully generated by your morphemes in a consistent order; any residue means the analysis is incomplete or wrong.
6. Check allomorph conditioning: for each morpheme with multiple shapes, state the rule choosing among them, phonological environment first, lexical listing only as a last resort.
7. State the morpheme-order template, for example subject-tense-root-object, and verify no attested form violates it.

8. Predict and verify: use the analysis to generate unattested forms, then check them against a speaker, a corpus, or a reference grammar; correct predictions are the strongest confirmation an analysis can earn.
9. Write the result as interlinear glossed text following the Leipzig Glossing Rules, so the analysis is transparent to any reader and falsifiable in detail.

sections.heading: Pitfalls, Hard Cases, and Open Questions
sections.body: Morphological analysis fails in characteristic ways, and knowing the failure modes is part of the training. The commonest error is segmentation by resemblance: seeing "ham" in "hamburger," a real historical mistake that speakers collectively made, or slicing "history" into "his story," a folk analysis with no etymological basis, since the word descends from Greek historia, "inquiry." The cure is the contrast test: a cut is licensed only if both pieces recur elsewhere with constant meaning. A second error is trusting spelling: English "-ed" is one spelling for three pronunciations, while the single sound sequence "er" spells at least four different morphemes, agentive "baker," comparative "bigger," and the unanalyzable endings of "father" and "water," plus dialectal fillers. A third is forcing exotic data into the mold of a familiar language, the trap early European grammarians fell into when they described Indigenous American and African languages through Latin's six cases; modern field method requires the language to reveal its own categories. A fourth is ignoring gradience: the boundary between compound and phrase, "ice cream" versus "nice cream," or between clitic and affix, such as the English possessive 's, which attaches to whole phrases in "the Queen of England's hat," resists clean lines, and honest analysis records the ambiguity rather than legislating it away. Genuine puzzles remain open at the research frontier. Where is the boundary between morphology and syntax, and does one even exist? Distributed Morphology says no; lexicalist theories say yes; phenomena like noun incorporation and Romance clitic clusters sit defiantly on the fence. Why is suffixing preferred worldwide, and how much of typology reflects processing pressure versus historical accident? What exactly does the brain store: full forms, stems, roots, schemas, or all of them redundantly, with usage constantly rebalancing the mixture, as race models suggest? How do children solve the segmentation problem from continuous speech with no labeled boundaries, a feat unsupervised algorithms still perform only imperfectly? And can any theory predict, rather than merely describe, which possible words a language will actually adopt? For the practical reader, the defenses against error are few and reliable. Demand recurrence before believing in a morpheme. Prefer the analysis with fewer arbitrary listings, but distrust an elegance that leaves residues unexplained. Treat frequency as evidence, since frequent forms behave differently from rare ones in storage, change, and judgment. Check etymology before asserting history, because synchronic structure and historical origin regularly diverge: "female" is unrelated to "male," reshaped from Old French femelle by attraction, and "island" took its silent s from unrelated "isle." Above all, remember that every speaker already possesses the system being described; the analyst's job is to make explicit what three-year-olds command implicitly. Done well, morphology turns the dictionary from a list into a map, showing not just which words exist but why they exist, what they are made of, and which words are waiting, fully licensed, to be spoken for the first time tomorrow.

guides.title: Grammatical Categories — Case, Gender, Number & Agreement
guides.summary: How languages use case, gender, number, and agreement to mark who does what to whom, how these systems work across the world's languages, and how they arise, change, and break down.

sections.heading: Why Grammatical Categories Matter
sections.body: Every sentence in every language must solve the same basic problem: the speaker has an event in mind, with participants playing different roles, and the hearer must reconstruct that scene from a stream of sounds or signs. Grammatical categories are the standardized, obligatory devices languages use to make that reconstruction reliable. Case marks the role a noun plays in its clause, distinguishing the dog that bites from the dog that is bitten. Gender sorts nouns into classes whose membership ripples through the rest of the sentence. Number tells the hearer how many entities are involved. Agreement ties these threads together, forcing words that belong together to display matching features, so a hearer can track who is being talked about even when word order is free. The linguist Roman Jakobson captured the essential point in 1959: languages differ not so much in what they can express as in what they must express. An English speaker may leave the sex of a friend unspecified; a French speaker choosing between ami and amie cannot. A Russian speaker must mark every noun for one of six cases; an English speaker marks case only on pronouns, in the contrast between I and me, or who and whom. Obligatory choices of this kind are grammatical categories in the strict sense: closed systems of options, one of which must be selected every time the relevant word class is used. Understanding them matters far beyond the classroom. Typologists use case and agreement systems to classify the world's roughly seven thousand languages and to reconstruct how they are historically related. Language learners struggle predictably with categories their native language lacks, which is why the German articles der, die, and das and the Russian case endings loom so large in second-language instruction. Translators constantly add information a source language leaves implicit, or discard information a target language cannot carry. Decipherers of ancient scripts, from Linear B to Hittite cuneiform, leaned heavily on recurring inflectional endings to crack the underlying grammar. Engineers building software that parses or generates human language must model agreement explicitly, because a system that produces the dogs barks betrays itself immediately. There is also a deeper scientific payoff. Grammatical categories look, at first glance, like arbitrary bookkeeping, yet they show striking regularities across unrelated languages: if a language has a dual number, it has a plural; if it marks gender on verbs, it marks gender on pronouns too. Such implicational universals, catalogued by Joseph Greenberg in the 1960s from a sample of thirty languages and refined by typologists ever since, suggest that the space of possible grammars is tightly constrained by how human memory, attention, and communication work. The categories also provide redundancy. Speech travels through noisy air, and endings that repeat the same information on article, adjective, and noun let a hearer recover a message even when part of it is masked by a cough or a passing truck. What looks like pointless complexity is often error-correcting code, refined by millennia of daily use.

sections.heading: Morphosyntactic Features and Inflection
sections.body: Linguists analyze categories such as case, gender, and number as features: named attributes that take one value from a small fixed set. Number is a feature with values such as singular and plural; case is a feature with values such as nominative and accusative; gender is a feature with values such as masculine, feminine, and neuter. A given word form then carries a bundle of feature values. The Latin form puellarum, for instance, simultaneously expresses the meaning girl, the case value genitive, and the number value plural. Features live at the border between morphology, the study of word structure, and syntax, the study of sentence structure, which is why they are called morphosyntactic: they are expressed inside words but they matter to relationships between words. The expression itself is called inflection, and it must be distinguished from derivation. Inflection produces forms of the same word, such as walk, walks, walked; derivation produces new words, such as walker from walk. Inflection is typically obligatory, regular, and does not change a word's part of speech; derivation is optional, gappy, and often does. Languages realize inflection through remarkably varied machinery, which linguists call exponence. The commonest device is affixation, adding prefixes or suffixes, as in English dog-s. Ablaut changes an internal vowel, as in sing, sang, sung, or goose and geese. Suppletion replaces the stem entirely: go and went, good and better. Tone can carry inflection, as in many West African languages where a verb's tense is signaled purely by pitch. Clitics, small words that lean phonologically on a neighbor like the English possessive in the queen of England's hat, occupy a middle ground between affix and free word. A single affix frequently expresses several features at once, a phenomenon called cumulative exponence: the Latin ending -orum in puellarum-style forms marks genitive and plural together, and no part of it can be assigned to one feature alone. The opposite arrangement, one neat affix per feature, is called agglutination and is typical of Turkish, Finnish, and Swahili, where a word like Turkish ev-ler-im-de, in my houses, stacks plural, possessor, and locative morphemes in strict order. Fusional languages like Latin and Russian bundle features cumulatively; isolating languages like Vietnamese and, increasingly, English express them with word order and separate particles instead; polysynthetic languages like Mohawk or Central Alaskan Yupik pack whole clauses worth of features into single enormous verbs. Zero exponence also exists: English sheep is plural in the sheep graze despite carrying no audible mark, and the plural value is revealed only by agreement. Finally, languages resort to periphrasis, multi-word constructions doing inflectional work, as when English expresses future time with will go because it lacks a future suffix. The lesson is that a category is defined by the distinctions it draws, not by any particular piece of sound that expresses it.

sections.heading: Case: Marking Who Does What to Whom
sections.body: Case is the grammatical category that marks a noun phrase for the role it plays relative to a verb or another head word. In the Latin sentence puella canem videt, the girl sees the dog, the ending -a on puella marks it as nominative, the subject, while -em on canem marks the object; reverse the endings and the dog sees the girl, no matter what order the words come in. That freedom is the central payoff of case: languages with rich case marking, such as Latin, Russian, Finnish, or Warlpiri, allow word order to be recruited for emphasis, contrast, and information flow, because the job of signaling grammatical roles is already done morphologically. Grammarians conventionally divide cases into two broad groups. Core or grammatical cases mark the central participants of a clause: nominative for subjects, accusative for direct objects, dative for recipients and beneficiaries, and genitive for possessors and other noun-to-noun relations, as in Latin liber puellae, the book of the girl. Peripheral, semantic, or local cases carry meanings that English handles with prepositions: instrumental for tools and means, locative for places, ablative for sources, allative for goals. The boundary between a case ending and an adposition is genuinely gradient. Japanese role markers like ga, o, and ni are written as separate particles but behave much like case suffixes; Hungarian endings such as -ban, meaning in, developed historically from postpositions and still show it. What counts is that the marker is obligatory, selected by grammar rather than free choice, and integrated into the noun's morphology. English retains only fragments of the Old English four-case system: the genitive clitic in the king's, and the subject-object contrast in pronouns, I versus me, she versus her, who versus whom. Everywhere else, fixed subject-verb-object order took over the work around the twelfth to fourteenth centuries as the old endings eroded. Case can also be sensitive to meaning in subtler ways. Many languages mark an object only when it is definite, animate, or otherwise prominent, a pattern called differential object marking. Spanish inserts a before human objects, veo a Maria but veo la casa; Turkish adds the accusative suffix -i only to definite objects, so kitap okudum means I read a book but kitabi okudum means I read the book; Hebrew uses the particle et under similar conditions. Case may additionally be governed rather than semantic: German prepositions dictate the case of their complement almost arbitrarily, mit taking dative and fuer taking accusative, while two-way prepositions like in take accusative for motion toward and dative for static location, ins Haus versus im Haus. Finally, case interacts with quantity and polarity: Russian and Finnish use genitive or partitive objects to express partial affectedness or negation, so Finnish contrasts join veden, I drank some water, in the partitive, with join veen, I drank the water up. Case, in short, is a compact interface between sentence structure and meaning.

sections.heading: Alignment Systems: Nominative, Ergative, and Beyond
sections.body: Comparing case systems across languages requires a neutral vocabulary, and typologists since R. M. W. Dixon use three labels: S for the single argument of an intransitive verb, as in she sleeps; A for the agent-like argument of a transitive verb; and P for the patient-like argument. Alignment is the question of which of these three a language groups together. Nominative-accusative languages, the type familiar from Latin, Russian, Japanese, and Turkish, treat S and A alike, calling both nominative, and single out P with the accusative. Ergative-absolutive languages instead treat S and P alike, in a case called absolutive that is usually unmarked, and single out A with the ergative. Basque works this way: gizona etorri da, the man came, leaves gizona bare, but gizonak ogia jan du, the man ate the bread, adds the ergative -k to the man while the bread stays bare. Roughly a quarter of the world's languages show ergative patterning somewhere, including Georgian, Hindi-Urdu, Tibetan, Mayan languages, and most languages of Australia. Pure systems are rare; splits are the norm. Hindi is ergative only in perfective aspect, so the boy in the boy ran carries no special mark, but in the boy ate the bread, when the verb is perfective, it takes the ergative postposition ne. Dyirbal, in Queensland, splits by person: first and second person pronouns run on a nominative-accusative basis while nouns run ergatively, a pattern predicted by Michael Silverstein's animacy hierarchy, which observes that the most speaker-like, human, definite participants resist ergative marking while the most thing-like resist accusative marking. Two rarer alignments complete the typology. Tripartite systems give S, A, and P three distinct marks, an arrangement attested in Nez Perce and in the Australian language Wangkumara; it is costly and correspondingly uncommon. Active-stative systems split intransitive S itself: agents of controlled actions like run are marked like A, while undergoers of uncontrolled events like fall or die are marked like P. Lakota and Georgian show versions of this split, sometimes called split intransitivity. It matters to keep morphology and syntax apart here. A language may mark case ergatively yet run its syntax, its rules for coordination and relative clauses, on a nominative-accusative basis; Warlpiri does exactly that. Dyirbal is the celebrated case of deep syntactic ergativity, where the pivot for linking clauses is the S/P grouping, so a sentence meaning mother saw father and returned is understood to mean that father returned. Alignment also shows up in verb agreement rather than case: many Mayan languages have no case on nouns at all but index A and P with distinct ergative and absolutive agreement prefixes on the verb. No alignment is more logical than another; each is a stable, self-consistent solution to the problem of distinguishing two participants in a transitive clause, and languages drift among them over historical time.

sections.heading: Case Inventories from Two to Twenty
sections.body: How many cases can a language have? The attested range is enormous. At the low end sit two-case systems: Old French preserved just a subject case and an oblique case from the Latin six, and modern standard Romanian distinguishes only a nominative-accusative form from a genitive-dative form in most nouns. English pronouns likewise oppose bare I, she, who to oblique me, her, whom, plus a possessive. German holds four cases, nominative, accusative, dative, genitive, carried mostly by articles and adjective endings rather than by nouns themselves. Icelandic keeps the same four with fuller noun morphology, plus famous quirks: certain verbs demand dative or even accusative subjects, as in mig dreymir, me dreams, meaning I dream. Russian has six productive cases, with remnants of a locative and a partitive hiding in fixed contexts; Latin counts six plus a marginal locative and a vocative used for direct address, as in Caesar's et tu, Brute, where Brute is the vocative of Brutus. Turkish also runs on six. The champions of case are found further east and north. Finnish grammars list fifteen cases, Hungarian grammars around eighteen, and the Northeast Caucasian languages Tsez, Lezgian, and Tabasaran are credited with several dozen. The trick behind such numbers is that most of the inventory is local cases built by combining two small feature sets: a location series, such as in, on, at, under, near, and a direction series, such as rest, motion toward, motion from, motion through. Multiply five locations by four directions and twenty distinct case labels appear, though each is composed of two transparent pieces. Finnish shows the logic clearly with its interior series, inessive talossa in the house, elative talosta out of the house, illative taloon into the house, matched by an exterior series, adessive, ablative, allative: talolla, talolta, talolle. Hungarian adds cases like the superessive for on top of and the sublative for onto. Whether one counts these as many cases or as a compact algebra is partly a matter of descriptive taste, which is why case counts should always be quoted with caution. Some languages even stack cases. In the Australian language Kayardild, a noun deep inside a phrase can wear up to four case suffixes at once, each copied down from a different layer of structure, and in Old Georgian and Hurrian a possessor noun takes its own genitive plus the case of the noun it modifies, a phenomenon called Suffixaufnahme. At the opposite extreme, languages like Mandarin Chinese, Vietnamese, and Yoruba have no case morphology whatsoever and rely on word order and prepositions. The broad statistical picture, visible in the World Atlas of Language Structures, is that large case inventories cluster in Eurasia and Australia, while case-poor languages dominate Southeast Asia, Africa, and much of the Americas.

sections.heading: Gender as a System of Noun Classes
sections.body: Grammatical gender is a system in which every noun belongs to one of a small number of classes, and that class membership is reflected on other words in the sentence. The reflection is the crucial part. The standard definition, articulated by Charles Hockett in 1958 and elaborated by Greville Corbett in his 1991 survey Gender, holds that genders are classes of nouns reflected in the behavior of associated words. A language that merely has words for male and female beings does not thereby have gender; a language has gender only if articles, adjectives, verbs, or pronouns change form depending on which noun they accompany. French has two genders: le livre vert, the green book, but la table verte, the green table, where both the article and the adjective shift. German and Russian have three, masculine, feminine, and neuter. Dutch and Swedish collapsed masculine and feminine into a common gender opposed to neuter. Many languages instead build gender on animacy: Algonquian languages such as Ojibwe divide nouns into animate and inanimate, and Danish dialects, Hittite, and many Dravidian systems draw similar lines. The word gender itself comes from Latin genus, meaning kind or sort, and only later narrowed in everyday English to mean sex; grammatical gender frequently has nothing to do with biology. Mark Twain's 1880 essay The Awful German Language made comedy of the fact that German Maedchen, girl, is neuter while Ruebe, turnip, is feminine, and the mismatch is real: assignment is a fact about nouns, not about the world. Still, in most gender languages there is a semantic core. Nouns denoting male humans are overwhelmingly masculine and nouns denoting female humans overwhelmingly feminine in French, Spanish, Russian, and Arabic; the rest of the vocabulary is distributed by formal rules and historical accident. Gender must also be separated from mere form. Spanish nouns in -a are usually feminine, but el dia, the day, is masculine, and la mano, the hand, is feminine, so the ending alone does not decide; what decides is the agreement the noun triggers. Linguists therefore diagnose gender by testing, never by translation: find the sets of nouns that demand the same forms of accompanying words, count the sets, and those are the genders. Covert gender exists too: English lost gender on nouns entirely, yet its pronouns he, she, and it still make a three-way semantic choice, a residue rather than a full system, since no article or adjective ever varies. The number of genders attested runs from two up through the teens when the term is extended to the large noun-class systems of Africa, and one language can change over time: Old English had the full three-gender Germanic system, and lost it between roughly 1000 and 1300 as the endings that carried it decayed.

sections.heading: How Nouns Get Their Gender
sections.body: If gender were purely arbitrary, children could only memorize it noun by noun, and borrowed words could never be assigned a class. In fact, assignment is governed by interacting rules, and Greville Corbett's cross-linguistic work shows they come in three kinds: semantic, morphological, and phonological. Some languages are almost purely semantic. In Tamil, nouns denoting male humans and gods are masculine, female humans and goddesses feminine, and everything else neuter; hearing a noun's meaning is enough to predict its class. Dyirbal, in northeast Australia, sorts nouns into four classes whose membership follows chains of cultural association: class two gathers women, fire, water, fighting, and dangerous creatures, the observation that gave George Lakoff the title of his 1987 book Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things. Other languages let morphology do the work. In Russian, a noun's declension class predicts its gender with high reliability: nouns ending in a hard consonant in the nominative singular are masculine, nouns in -a are feminine, nouns in -o or -e are neuter, and the semantic rule overrides the formal one only for nouns like papa, dad, which declines like a feminine but takes masculine agreement because it denotes a male. Phonological assignment is exemplified by Qafar, spoken in Ethiopia and Djibouti, where nouns ending in an accented vowel are feminine and the rest are masculine, a rule that sorts nearly the whole lexicon. French sits in between: the final sounds of a word predict gender statistically rather than absolutely. Endings spelled -tion, -sion, and -te are feminine well over ninety-five percent of the time, while -age and -eau run strongly masculine; experiments by Tucker, Lambert, and Rigault in the 1970s showed that French speakers apply these probabilities to invented words they have never heard. Borrowings prove the rules are alive. When English weekend entered French it became le week-end, masculine, the default class; German assigned das Baby neuter matching semantic rules for young beings. Loanwords may take gender from their form, from a native synonym, or from a default class, and watching which wins is a standard probe of a language's assignment hierarchy. Defaults matter within the native vocabulary too: when Russian speakers meet an indeclinable loan like taksi, taxi, formal rules cannot apply and the word settles into neuter, the residue class. None of this makes assignment fully predictable everywhere. German gender is notoriously leaky, with rules covering perhaps eighty percent of nouns and the rest genuinely memorized, and psycholinguistic evidence shows native speakers store gender as part of each noun's lexical entry, retrieving it faster than they could compute it. The practical consequence for learners is unglamorous but well supported: learn every noun together with its article from the first encounter, and let the statistical rules serve as a safety net rather than a substitute for memory.

sections.heading: Noun Classes and Classifiers Beyond Europe
sections.body: The two- and three-gender systems of Europe are a small corner of a much larger design space. The Bantu languages of central, eastern, and southern Africa, some five hundred of them including Swahili, Zulu, and Lingala, organize nouns into systems traditionally counted at up to eighteen or more classes, each marked by a prefix on the noun and echoed by prefixes across the sentence. In Swahili, class one and class two pair off as singular and plural for humans: mtu, person, watu, people. Classes seven and eight handle many artifacts: kitabu, book, vitabu, books. A sentence like kitabu kikubwa kimeanguka, the big book fell, repeats the class marker ki- on the adjective and the verb, giving alliterative concord that makes reference tracking extraordinarily robust. Because singular and plural pairings are part of the system, Bantuists count classes rather than genders, but the mechanism, obligatory noun classification reflected by agreement, is exactly gender writ large. Comparable systems appear in Australia, where Yanyuwa has been described with around sixteen classes, and in the Niger-Congo language Fula, whose twenty-odd classes trigger consonant changes at the start of the noun itself. A different strategy altogether is the numeral classifier system typical of East and Southeast Asia. Mandarin Chinese nouns have no gender and no plural marking, but counting requires a measure word matched to the noun's shape or kind: san ben shu, three volume book, for books; liang zhang zhuozi, two flat-thing table, for tables; yi tiao yu, one long-thing fish. Japanese counters work the same way, with -hon for long thin objects, -mai for flat ones, -hiki for small animals; Thai, Vietnamese, Korean, and many Mayan and Amazonian languages have parallel inventories running from a handful to well over a hundred classifiers. Classifiers resemble gender in sorting nouns by kind, but they differ on the diagnostic property: they do not trigger agreement. A Mandarin classifier appears once, next to the numeral, and no other word in the sentence changes form because of it. Classifier choice is also somewhat fluid, letting speakers recategorize an object for expressive effect, whereas gender is fixed per noun. The two systems can coexist and can feed each other historically; classifiers that become obligatory and start controlling agreement are one attested source of new gender systems, a path documented in languages of the Amazon such as Miraña. Sign languages add a further variant: in American Sign Language, classifier handshapes standing for vehicles, upright beings, or flat surfaces are incorporated into verbs of motion and location, categorizing referents inside the verb itself. The general lesson of this diversity is that obligatory noun categorization is a recurring solution to the problem of keeping track of what is being talked about, and languages differ mainly in where they hang the marks: on the noun, on its neighbors, or on the numeral.

sections.heading: Number: Singular, Plural, and the Spaces Between
sections.body: Number is the grammatical category that encodes quantity of referents, and English gives the misleading impression that the only options are one versus more than one. The cross-linguistic menu is richer. Many languages add a dual, a form specifically for two: Slovene and Upper Sorbian keep the old Indo-European dual alive, so a Slovene speaker distinguishes ena miza, one table, dve mizi, two tables, and tri mize, three tables; Modern Standard Arabic builds duals productively with -aan, as in kitabaan, two books; Ancient Greek and Sanskrit had duals, and traces survive in English both and either, which apply only to pairs. Rarer still is the trial, a form for exactly three, found in pronoun systems of Austronesian and Oceanic languages such as Larike in Indonesia and Tok Pisin's pronoun set, where mitripela means the three of us. No language is reliably reported with a grammatical quadral. Some languages have a paucal instead, meaning a few: Bayso, in Ethiopia, contrasts singular, paucal, and plural on nouns, and Fijian and many Oceanic languages show paucal pronouns. Greenberg's universal number thirty-four states the implicational chain: no language has a trial without a dual, and none has a dual without a plural. There are also greater plurals for unusually large multitudes, attested in Fula and Hausa descriptions, and associative plurals meaning X and those associated with X, like Hungarian Jánosék, John and his family or crowd, and Japanese Tanaka-tachi. Equally important is what a language does when it does not mark number. Japanese, Mandarin, and Korean nouns are transnumeral: hon in Japanese means book or books, with quantity left to context or numeral phrases, and this is not impoverishment but a different division of labor. English itself splits its vocabulary into count nouns, which pluralize, and mass nouns like water, rice, and furniture, which resist counting directly and need measure phrases such as three pieces of furniture. The count-mass line is partly conceptual and partly conventional, as the contrast between English furniture, uncountable, and French meubles, countable, shows. Morphologically, plurals form in every way inflection can: suffixes as in dog-s; umlaut as in goose, geese, a vowel change caused historically by a lost plural ending that fronted the stem vowel; the -en of oxen and children preserving an old weak declension; reduplication, as in Indonesian buku-buku, books; and the templatic broken plurals of Arabic, where kitaab, book, becomes kutub, books, by re-vowelling the consonantal root. Irregular plurals cluster among the most frequent nouns because frequency shields forms from analogical regularization. There are also pluralia tantum, nouns that exist only in the plural like scissors, trousers, and oats, and singularia tantum like news and physics that look plural but take singular agreement. Number thus turns out to be a small category with intricate edges, and those edges, universals, gaps, and irregularities, carry much of the evidence about how speakers store and generalize grammar.

sections.heading: Agreement: The Mechanism of Feature Copying
sections.body: Agreement, also called concord, is the phenomenon in which the form of one word is determined by the grammatical features of another. In she walks, the verb carries -s because the subject is third person singular; in Spanish las casas blancas, the white houses, the article and the adjective both display feminine plural because the noun casa is feminine and pluralized. Corbett's standard terminology names the parts: the controller is the element whose features are copied, typically a noun phrase; the target is the word that changes form, such as a verb, adjective, article, demonstrative, or pronoun; the domain is the syntactic stretch within which the copying holds, such as the clause for subject-verb agreement or the noun phrase for concord; and the features are the categories copied, person, number, gender, and in some languages case. Targets vary enormously across languages. English confines productive agreement to one corner, the present-tense third singular -s, plus the forms of be. Romance and Slavic languages spread gender and number across articles, adjectives, participles, and predicate nominals. Swahili verbs carry a subject prefix and, under definiteness conditions, an object prefix, so a single verb form like a-li-ki-soma encodes that a class-one subject read a class-seven object in the past. Hungarian verbs agree not only with the subject but with the definiteness of the object, distinguishing olvasok, I read something, from olvasom, I read it. Some Caucasian languages show long-distance agreement, where a matrix verb agrees with an argument inside an embedded clause, a configuration Tsez made famous in the theoretical literature. Sign languages realize agreement spatially: in American Sign Language, verbs like GIVE move from the location assigned to the giver toward the location assigned to the recipient, copying referential indices through space rather than sound. Formally, agreement is modeled in two broad ways. Unification-based frameworks such as HPSG and LFG treat controller and target as jointly constraining a shared feature bundle, which must be consistent; the derivational tradition of generative grammar treats agreement as an operation, Agree, in which a probe, say a tense head, searches its domain for a goal bearing matching features and copies their values. For a working analyst the frameworks converge on the same descriptive discipline: state which features are copied, from what, onto what, and within what domain. Functionally, agreement earns its keep twice over. It is redundancy, protecting the message against noise, and it is a reference tracking device, letting a hearer link a distant pronoun or verb back to the right participant. That second job explains a robust typological observation: languages with rich agreement often allow pronouns to be dropped entirely, as Spanish and Italian do, because the verb ending already identifies the subject. The agreement morphology is, in effect, a pronoun absorbed into the verb, and historically that is usually exactly what it was.

sections.heading: Controllers, Targets, and the Agreement Hierarchy
sections.body: Agreement would be simple if features were always copied mechanically, but the interesting cases are those where grammar and meaning pull apart. British English speakers say the committee has decided when they view the committee as a unit, and the committee have decided when they view it as a collection of people; American English strongly prefers the singular. German Maedchen, girl, is grammatically neuter, and within its own noun phrase the agreement is rigidly neuter, das Maedchen; but a following pronoun may be either es, matching the grammar, or sie, matching the meaning. Russian vrach, doctor, is masculine in form, yet when it refers to a woman, speakers increasingly say vrach prishla, with a feminine verb. Such hybrid nouns behave with lawlike regularity captured by Corbett's Agreement Hierarchy, formulated in 1979. Arrange targets on a scale: attributive modifier, then predicate, then relative pronoun, then personal pronoun. As one moves rightward along the scale, agreement according to meaning becomes monotonically more likely, and agreement according to form less likely. No language allows semantic agreement on the attributive adjective while demanding formal agreement on the distant pronoun; the reverse pattern is common everywhere. The hierarchy is one of the best-supported generalizations in morphosyntax and gives fieldworkers a sharp prediction to test. A second classic problem is resolution: what features does a target show when its controller is a conjunction of mismatched nouns? Languages adopt explicit rules. French resolves mixed masculine and feminine conjuncts to masculine plural, the rule generations of schoolchildren learned as masculine prevails; Slovene resolves two singular conjuncts to dual; Slavic and Bantu languages have detailed gender resolution rules, with Luganda resolving human plus nonhuman conjuncts to a human class. An alternative strategy is closest-conjunct agreement, where the verb or adjective simply agrees with the nearest conjunct and ignores the rest; Arabic verbs before conjoined subjects and many English speakers in sentences like there is a table and two chairs show exactly this. Politeness systems create further principled mismatches: French vous addressed to one respected person takes plural verb agreement but singular predicate adjectives, vous etes gentil, you are kind, with gentil singular; German Sie takes third plural verbs for a second person singular meaning. Quantified expressions add their own friction, as in English a number of issues remain, where the notional plural wins over the singular head noun number. The practical moral for analysis is to treat mismatches not as noise but as structured data. When agreement wobbles, record which target wobbles, in which direction, and how often; the wobble almost always lines up with the hierarchy, with animacy, or with distance, and it is frequently the leading edge of a change in progress, as formal gender gives way to semantic reference one target type at a time.

sections.heading: Paradigms, Declensions, and Syncretism
sections.body: The full set of inflected forms of a word, arranged by feature values, is its paradigm, and paradigms are where the abstract categories meet the concrete facts of a language. Latin puella runs through puella, puellam, puellae, and so on across six cases and two numbers; the verb amare fills roughly a hundred and twenty cells across tense, mood, voice, person, and number. Nouns that inflect the same way form a declension class, verbs a conjugation class. Latin has five declensions, Russian three main ones, Old English around a dozen counting minor types. The unsettling property of inflection classes is that membership usually means nothing: there is no semantic difference between a Latin second declension noun and a third declension noun; the class merely dictates which endings to use. Such purely formal organization, morphology by itself, was called morphomic by Mark Aronoff in 1994, and it poses a real puzzle for theories that want every grammatical distinction to carry meaning. Learners cope because classes are signaled by cues, such as the nominative and genitive singular pair that Latin dictionaries list as principal parts, from which the rest of the paradigm is projectable. Paradigms are also full of systematic gaps and overlaps. Syncretism is the collapse of distinct feature combinations into one form: German die serves as nominative and accusative for feminines and for all plurals; Russian feminine nouns use one form for dative and prepositional singular; English you is simultaneously singular, plural, subject, and object, the maximal syncretism produced when thou was lost. Syncretism is not random; it targets natural classes of cells and often persists for centuries as an organizing fact of the language. Defectiveness is the outright absence of a form: Russian famously lacks an acceptable first person singular future of pobedit, to win, so speakers must paraphrase; Latin vis, force, lacks a genuine genitive plural in classical usage; French frit, fried, historically lacked parts of its verb paradigm. Deponency is a mismatch between form and function, as in Latin verbs like hortari, to urge, which are passive in form but active in meaning throughout. Suppletion stitches a paradigm together from unrelated stems, as in go and went, where went was historically the past of wend, or good, better, best. Frequency is the guardian of all this irregularity: the most used words, be, go, have, the personal pronouns, tolerate the strangest paradigms because constant use keeps them memorized, while rare words drift toward the regular pattern by analogy. For anyone documenting or learning a language, the paradigm is therefore the fundamental unit of description: elicit whole tables rather than isolated forms, note which cells fall together, which are missing, and which are built from different stems, because those patterns are stable, diagnostic, and historically revealing.

sections.heading: How Categories Are Born and How They Die
sections.body: Grammatical categories are not eternal; they are created, reshaped, and destroyed by ordinary language change, and the life cycle is well documented. The creative engine is grammaticalization, the process by which independent words bleach in meaning, erode in form, and harden into grammatical markers. Case endings routinely descend from adpositions, and adpositions in turn from nouns and verbs; Hungarian -ban, in, comes from an old noun meaning interior, and the Japanese particle no, genitive, traces to a demonstrative construction. Verb agreement descends most often from pronouns: a pronoun habitually repeated next to the verb, as in a topic construction like John, he-came, fuses onto it, and the attested chain runs pronoun to clitic to obligatory affix. French spoken colloquially is arguably partway through this cycle again, with subject clitics like je and il behaving increasingly like prefixes. Gender systems arise when demonstratives or classifiers that sort nouns become obligatory and start being echoed on other words, a path observed in Amazonian and Papuan languages. The destructive engine is sound change, which is blind to grammar. Late Latin lost final -m and merged unstressed vowels, collapsing the six-case system into the two-case system of Old French and eventually the caseless Romance of today, with prepositions like de and ad taking over the work of genitive and dative. English tells the same story compounded by contact: Old English had four cases, three genders, and rich verb agreement, but the Viking-age contact between Old English and Old Norse speakers, whose words shared stems while differing in endings, accelerated the loss of inflection across the North of England, and fixed word order plus prepositions absorbed the functions. When erosion outpaces repair, analogy steps in to tidy the wreckage, leveling paradigms by extending one stem or ending at the expense of others, which is how child forms like foots arise and how historical English replaced kine with cows. Categories can also be reanalyzed rather than lost: the Hindi ergative case arose when a Sanskrit passive participle construction, of the type the bread was eaten by the boy, was reinterpreted as an ordinary transitive clause, leaving the old instrumental agent marker stranded as an ergative. Creole languages, born from abrupt contact, typically start with little or no case, gender, or agreement, and some, given centuries, begin rebuilding them, which suggests these categories are cheap to lose and slow to grow. Two practical corollaries follow. First, irregularity is fossil evidence: umlaut plurals and suppletive verbs preserve sound changes and old classes that regular vocabulary has erased, so historical linguists mine exactly the forms learners curse. Second, no stage of a language is corrupt or degenerate; the caseless English of today and the case-heavy English of the year 900 are equally functional solutions, snapshots of one system rebalancing itself.

sections.heading: Learning and Processing Grammatical Categories
sections.body: How do human minds acquire and use these systems in real time? Children are strikingly good at them. Learners of rich gender languages such as Russian, German, or Swahili control most of the system by age three or four, using the phonological and morphological cues of nouns to generalize, and their errors are overwhelmingly sensible overgeneralizations rather than random noise. The classic demonstration is Jean Berko's 1958 wug test: shown a novel creature called a wug and asked about two of them, English-speaking preschoolers reliably say wugs, proving they command a productive rule rather than a memorized list. The same productivity produces errors like goed and foots, which appear precisely when a child's rule machinery overrides stored irregulars and then recede as memory strengthens. Adult second-language learners face a different landscape. Categories absent from the first language are persistently hard: gender assignment and agreement remain error-prone even in near-native speakers who began learning after childhood, and learners whose first language has gender transfer their expectations, helpfully or not. Case systems yield to explicit instruction more readily than gender does, perhaps because case aligns with meaning while gender must be memorized per noun. Adult native processing shows agreement operating fast and automatically. In electroencephalography experiments, agreement violations like the boys runs evoke a characteristic brain response, a late positive wave around six hundred milliseconds known as the P600, and gender mismatches in article-noun pairs do the same in Spanish, German, and Dutch. Behavioral work shows gender priming: hearing la in Spanish speeds recognition of upcoming feminine nouns, meaning listeners use agreement predictively, not just as after-the-fact checking. Production has its signature failure, agreement attraction, first studied systematically by Kathryn Bock and Carol Miller in 1991: speakers asked to continue preambles like the key to the cabinets frequently produce are, letting the nearby plural cabinets hijack the verb even though the subject is singular. Attraction is robust across languages, is strongest when the interfering noun is plural, and reveals that agreement in real time consults a noisy memory representation of the sentence rather than a clean syntactic tree. Comprehenders show a matching blind spot, often failing to notice attraction errors in reading. Aphasia completes the picture: agrammatic speakers with damage to left frontal regions tend to omit or simplify inflection, yet frequently preserve knowledge of gender, suggesting that stored lexical features and the machinery that deploys them can dissociate. Two general lessons emerge. First, obligatory categories are processed as habits, deeply automatized, which is why they resist late learning and why native errors are systematic rather than arbitrary. Second, the categories earn their processing cost: prediction experiments show that gender, number, and case marking measurably speed comprehension, confirming the functional story that these systems buy the listener time and certainty.

sections.heading: Mismatches, Pitfalls, and Sound Analytical Practice
sections.body: Anyone working with grammatical categories, whether learning a language, documenting one, or building software around one, meets the same recurring failure modes, and most have known remedies. The first trap is translation-equivalence: assuming that a category in one language maps onto a category in another because the textbook uses the same name. The German dative is not the Latin dative; the Japanese particle ga is not a nominative ending in the Latin sense; Swahili noun classes are not masculine and feminine in disguise. The remedy is to define every category language-internally, by the distinctions and agreements actually observed, and to use interlinear glossing conventions such as the Leipzig Glossing Rules, which force the analyst to label each morpheme explicitly and expose hidden assumptions immediately. The second trap is diagnosing gender from noun form rather than from agreement: Spanish la mano and el dia, or Russian papa, demonstrate that the shape of the noun can lie, while agreement targets tell the truth. Always test with an article, adjective, or verb before declaring a noun's class. The third trap is treating variation as error. Committee are, the key to the cabinets are, vous etes gentil, vrach prishla: each looks like a mistake against a school rule, yet each is systematic, predicted by the Agreement Hierarchy, by attraction, or by politeness grammar, and several are changes in progress. Record the variation with its conditions instead of correcting it away. The fourth trap is boundary disputes handled dogmatically: case ending versus postposition, gender versus classifier, dual versus paucal are gradient distinctions, and honest description says so rather than forcing a clean label. Fifth, beware of paradigm gaps and syncretism when eliciting: a fieldworker who asks for one form per cell can miss that two cells are systematically identical, or that a cell is missing altogether, so elicit full tables and cross-check with sentences that force agreement to reveal covert features, the way the sheep graze reveals plurality that the bare noun hides. For learners the practical program follows directly from the mechanisms. Memorize gender with each noun from day one, using the article as part of the word. Learn case as meaning first, endings second, organizing drills around functions such as recipient or instrument. Expect and forgive attraction errors in your own speech, since natives make them too. For engineers, the corresponding rules are to store features in the lexicon, to implement agreement as constraint checking rather than string matching, and to test on conjoined subjects, collective nouns, and politeness pronouns, exactly where naive systems fail. And when an analysis stops working, when agreement data contradict the gender assignments or a case refuses to fit the inventory, treat that as information: it usually means a hybrid noun, a change in progress, or a category boundary drawn in the wrong place, and it is precisely how the field's best generalizations, from Greenberg's universals to the Agreement Hierarchy, were found in the first place.

guides.title: Syntax — How Sentences Work
guides.summary: A complete account of sentence structure: how words group into phrases, how phrases nest into hierarchical trees, how verbs demand their arguments, why word order differs across languages, how questions and passives displace material, and what the constraints on all of this reveal about the human language faculty.

sections.heading: What Syntax Is and Why It Matters
sections.body: Syntax is the system that decides which strings of words count as sentences of a language and what those sentences mean structurally. It is not spelling, not punctuation, not vocabulary, and not the etiquette of formal writing. It is the largely unconscious machinery that lets a five-year-old who has never heard the sentence "the purple crocodile that ate my homework apologised twice" understand it instantly, and equally lets that child reject "crocodile the purple homework my ate that twice apologised" as not English at all. Neither string has ever been encountered before. Neither can be handled by memory. Something generative is at work. The central fact syntax exists to explain is often called discrete infinity: a finite brain, a finite vocabulary of perhaps 30,000 to 60,000 words for an educated adult, and a finite set of rules, yet an unbounded set of possible sentences. You can always insert one more adjective, one more relative clause, one more "I think that". There is no longest sentence in English in the way there is no largest integer. This rules out any account of language as a list of memorised expressions, and forces an account in terms of combination — small pieces assembled by rules into larger pieces, recursively. The second central fact is that meaning depends on structure, not merely on order. Consider "the police shot the rioters with rifles". If the rifles belong to the police, they are the instrument of shooting; if they belong to the rioters, they merely describe who was shot. The words are identical and in identical order. Only the invisible grouping differs. This is structural ambiguity, and it is the single most persuasive demonstration that sentences have hidden architecture. Every reader resolves such sentences constantly without noticing. A third fact is that syntactic knowledge is largely tacit. Native speakers can judge, with speed and striking agreement, that "who did you say that left?" is bad while "who did you say left?" is fine, yet almost none can state the rule involved. Linguists therefore treat grammaticality judgements as data about the mind, much as a physicist treats meter readings as data about the world, marking unacceptable strings with an asterisk. The judgements are noisy at the margins and vary by dialect, and there is genuine ongoing debate about how reliable introspective judgements are compared with large corpus counts or controlled acceptability experiments; the honest position is that all three sources are used and mostly converge. Why does this matter practically? Because syntax underlies every technology that processes language, every account of how children acquire speech, every clinical description of aphasia after stroke, every translation problem, and every serious attempt to write clearly. Understanding structure turns "this sentence feels wrong" into a diagnosis you can act on.

sections.heading: Constituents — Finding the Groups Inside a Sentence
sections.body: The foundational move in syntax is discovering that a sentence is not a flat chain of words but a nested set of groups called constituents. A constituent is any stretch of words that behaves as a single unit for the purposes of the grammar. In "the old dog on the porch barked loudly", the words "the old dog on the porch" form one unit, and "barked loudly" another; "dog on the" is not a unit at all, even though the words are adjacent. Constituency is not decided by intuition alone. Linguists use a battery of diagnostic tests, and a string that passes several of them is almost certainly a genuine constituent. The substitution test replaces a candidate string with a single pro-form: "the old dog on the porch" can be replaced by "it", and the sentence survives, whereas nothing can replace "dog on the". The movement or topicalisation test fronts the string: "on the porch, the old dog barked" is fine, so "on the porch" is a unit. The coordination test conjoins the candidate with a like element using "and": "the old dog on the porch and the cat in the window barked" works, so each conjunct is a constituent. The question-answer or fragment test asks whether the string can stand alone as an answer: to "what barked?" you may reply "the old dog on the porch", which is a full and natural fragment, but you may not reply "dog on the". The clefting test embeds the string in "it was ___ that ...": "it was the old dog on the porch that barked" is grammatical. These tests are tools, not oracles, and they sometimes disagree. Some genuine constituents resist movement; some non-constituents can be coordinated in special elliptical constructions such as "John gave Mary a book and Bill a record", where "Bill a record" is not obviously a unit under classical assumptions. Such cases are actively debated and have driven whole theoretical frameworks. The practical rule is convergence: if three or four independent tests agree, treat the string as a constituent. The reason constituency matters so much is that all further syntactic statements are stated over constituents. Rules do not refer to "the third word" or "everything before the verb"; they refer to "the subject noun phrase" or "the complement clause". Structure-dependence, as it is called, is one of the most robust findings in the field: no known human language forms questions by, say, reversing the linear order of words or fronting the fourth word. Instead, operations target structural units. Children appear to assume this from the start, rarely producing errors that would follow from a purely linear rule, which has been taken as evidence that structure-dependence is not learned from data but built into the architecture of the language faculty — a claim that remains contested but that no competing account has fully dissolved.

sections.heading: Phrases and Heads — the Architecture Every Phrase Shares
sections.body: Constituents come in types, and each type is organised around one obligatory word called the head. Before the head can be identified, its word class must be, and here traditional definitions fail badly. A noun is not "a person, place or thing" — "destruction", "arrival" and "honesty" are nouns denoting events and properties — and a verb is not "an action word", since "own", "cost" and "resemble" denote no action. Syntax defines classes distributionally, by where a word can occur: a noun is what can follow a determiner, pluralise and head a subject; a verb is what can carry tense and follow "must"; an adjective is what can sit between a determiner and a noun and take "very". Alongside these open classes sit small closed classes — determiners, auxiliaries, complementisers, conjunctions, prepositions — that carry the structural skeleton, are enormously frequent ("the" alone is about 6 percent of running English text), and are disproportionately lost in agrammatic aphasia. The head determines the category and much of the behaviour of the whole phrase. In the noun phrase "the enormous crate of overripe mangoes", the head is "crate": the phrase refers to a crate, it takes singular agreement because "crate" is singular ("the crate of mangoes is heavy", not "are heavy"), In "walked slowly toward the river", the head is the verb "walked". In "extremely fond of jazz", the head is the adjective "fond". In "just after midnight", the head is the preposition "after". A phrase is named for its head: noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, prepositional phrase, usually abbreviated NP, VP, AP, PP. Around the head, three structural positions recur so consistently across categories and across languages that they were generalised into a template known as X-bar theory, developed in the late 1960s and 1970s. Written with X standing for any category, the schema says a phrase XP consists of a specifier plus an intermediate projection X-bar, which in turn consists of the head plus its complements, with adjuncts attaching to X-bar. The vocabulary matters less than the three-way distinction it encodes. The complement is the phrase the head selects and is closest to it: "of overripe mangoes" completes "crate", "the river" completes "toward", "of jazz" completes "fond". Complements are typically obligatory or strongly expected, they sit adjacent to the head, and there is normally only one. Adjuncts are optional modifiers that can stack indefinitely: "the crate of mangoes in the hold from Manila that we bought yesterday". You can pile adjuncts on freely, and they generally attach outside complements, which is why "the crate in the hold of mangoes" sounds wrong. The specifier is the outermost element, typically one per phrase: the determiner "the" for nouns, "extremely" for the adjective, and in classical accounts the subject for the verb phrase. This uniformity matters because the child need not learn a separate blueprint for each category: learn that phrases have heads, complements, adjuncts and specifiers, and only a few parameters remain to be fixed per language — chiefly whether heads precede their complements, as in English and Swahili, or follow them, as in Japanese and Turkish.

sections.heading: Trees, Hierarchy and Structural Ambiguity
sections.body: Once constituents and heads are established, a sentence can be drawn as a tree: a diagram in which the whole sentence sits at the top, branches divide into its immediate constituents, and those divide again until individual words are reached at the bottom. Equivalently the structure can be written with labelled brackets, so "the dog chased a cat" becomes [S [NP the dog] [VP chased [NP a cat]]]. Trees are not decoration. They encode three claims simultaneously: which words group together, what category each group is, and which groups are inside which others. The vocabulary of trees is worth learning because syntactic rules are stated in it. A node immediately above another dominates it; a node above at any distance dominates it too. Two nodes with the same mother are sisters. The relation that does most of the work is c-command, introduced by Tanya Reinhart in 1976: a node c-commands its sisters and everything inside them. C-command turns out to be the relation that governs pronoun reference, negative polarity licensing, and quantifier scope, which is a striking result — several apparently unrelated phenomena all turn out to obey the same structural condition. Structural ambiguity is the clearest empirical payoff. "Visiting relatives can be tiresome" has two structures: one where "visiting" is a verb and "relatives" its object, meaning that going to see them is tiresome, and one where "visiting" modifies "relatives", meaning that relatives who visit are tiresome. "I saw the man with the telescope" attaches the prepositional phrase either to the verb phrase, giving the instrument reading, or to the noun phrase, giving the reading where the man possesses the telescope. "Old men and women" either has "old" scoping over both nouns or only over "men". Newspaper headlines exploit this accidentally with famous results: "British left waffles on Falklands", "Squad helps dog bite victim", "Complaints about NBA referees growing ugly". Attachment ambiguity has measurable psychological consequences. Reading-time experiments show that readers systematically prefer certain attachments, and that violating the preference costs measurable milliseconds and sometimes causes conscious breakdown. The best-known example is the garden-path sentence: "the horse raced past the barn fell" is fully grammatical — the horse that was raced past the barn fell — but almost every reader initially parses "raced" as the main verb and crashes at "fell". Others include "the old man the boats" and "the cotton clothing is made of grows in Mississippi". These sentences show that the parser commits to a structure incrementally, word by word, rather than waiting for the end. Ambiguity also compounds combinatorially. A sentence with n prepositional phrases in sequence has a number of possible attachment structures given by the Catalan numbers: 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132. "I saw the man in the park with the telescope on the hill" has 14 parses in principle. Human listeners almost never notice, because context, plausibility and prosody prune the space instantly — but any computer parser must confront the full explosion, which is why statistical disambiguation became the central problem of computational syntax.

sections.heading: Subjects, Objects and Grammatical Functions
sections.body: Constituent structure tells you how words group; grammatical functions tell you what role each group plays. The main functions are subject, direct object, indirect object, predicative complement and oblique. These are relational notions — a noun phrase is not intrinsically a subject, it is the subject of a particular clause — and they cut across both structure and meaning. In English the subject is identified by a cluster of properties rather than a single one. It normally precedes the verb in declaratives; it inverts with the auxiliary in questions ("has she left?"); it controls verb agreement ("she walks" versus "they walk"); it appears in nominative form if it is a pronoun ("she", not "her"); it is the understood subject of an infinitive ("she wants to leave"); and it is the element that a tag question echoes ("she left, didn't she?"). Applying several of these tests together handles awkward cases. In "there are three problems", the tests point to "there" as the grammatical subject even though "three problems" carries the meaning and, oddly, controls the agreement — a genuine mismatch that theories handle in different ways. The direct object is the phrase that follows the verb without a preposition, becomes the subject under passivisation, and appears in accusative case for pronouns. This last diagnostic is nearly invisible in English, which marks case only on seven pronoun pairs (I/me, he/him, she/her, we/us, they/them, who/whom, and the vestigial thou/thee). Languages with rich case morphology make functions explicit on the noun itself: Latin, Russian, Finnish, Turkish and Hungarian all mark subject and object distinctly, and consequently permit far freer word order, because the case ending rather than the position identifies the role. Finnish has around fifteen cases; Hungarian is usually counted at eighteen; Latin uses six. It is essential to keep grammatical function separate from semantic role. In "the window broke", "the window" is the subject but semantically the thing affected, not an agent. In "the key opened the door", "the key" is subject but instrument. In "Sandra received a letter", she is subject but recipient. Conversely, in the passive "the door was opened by the key", the same instrument appears in an oblique phrase. Function and role are systematically related but not identical, and much of syntactic theory concerns exactly how one maps onto the other. Languages also differ in how they align these categories. English and most European languages are nominative-accusative: the single argument of an intransitive verb is treated like the agent of a transitive one. Ergative-absolutive languages, including Basque, Dyirbal, Georgian in some tenses, and many Mayan languages, treat the single intransitive argument like the object of a transitive verb instead, marking the transitive agent specially. Roughly a quarter of the world's languages show ergative patterning somewhere in their grammar, often only in certain tenses or only in the morphology and not the syntax — so-called split ergativity.

sections.heading: Verbs and Their Arguments — Valency and Theta Roles
sections.body: The verb is the organising centre of the clause, and its most consequential property is valency: how many arguments it requires and of what kind. "Sleep" is intransitive and takes one argument, the sleeper. "Devour" is transitive and requires two: "she devoured the pie", never "*she devoured". "Give" is ditransitive and requires three: giver, thing given, recipient. "Put" requires three of a different shape: agent, theme and location, and refuses to do without the location, which is why "*I put the book" is impossible where "*I gave the book" is merely elliptical. Each argument is assigned a semantic role, often called a theta role or thematic role. The standard inventory includes agent, the deliberate instigator; patient or theme, the entity affected or moved; experiencer, the one who perceives or feels; recipient and goal; source; instrument; beneficiary; and location. A widely assumed principle, the theta criterion in Chomskyan work, holds that each argument receives exactly one role and each role is assigned to exactly one argument. This immediately explains why "*she devoured the pie the cake" is ungrammatical: there is no second role available for the extra noun phrase. Verbs also select the syntactic category of their complements, a property called subcategorisation, and this is independent of theta roles. "Wonder" takes a question complement ("she wondered whether it rained") but not a noun phrase ("*she wondered the rain"). "Doubt" takes both. "Seem" takes a clause or an adjective but not a bare noun phrase. "Persuade" takes an object plus an infinitive ("persuade her to go"), while "promise" takes the same surface shape but assigns the infinitive's subject differently — in "she promised him to go", the goer is she, whereas in "she persuaded him to go" the goer is him. Children reliably misinterpret "promise" until around age six, a finding from Carol Chomsky's 1969 work that has been replicated many times. The same verb often permits several frames, and the alternations are systematic rather than random. The dative alternation pairs "give the book to Mary" with "give Mary the book", but it is restricted by an odd morphological condition: native Germanic verbs alternate freely, Latinate ones resist, so "tell her the news" is fine while "*explain her the news" is not for most speakers. The causative alternation pairs "the ice melted" with "the sun melted the ice", and applies to verbs of change of state but not to "*the pie devoured". The locative alternation pairs "load hay onto the wagon" with "load the wagon with hay", and the two differ in meaning: the second implies the wagon is full, an effect called the holistic interpretation. Learning these idiosyncratic restrictions poses a genuine puzzle, since children rarely receive explicit correction, and it remains one of the liveliest debates in acquisition research.

sections.heading: Word Order — Typology and the Head Parameter
sections.body: Given a subject, a verb and an object, there are six logically possible orders, and the world's languages are distributed among them with striking unevenness. Drawing on the World Atlas of Language Structures survey of over 1,300 languages, subject-object-verb order accounts for roughly 41 percent and subject-verb-object for roughly 35 percent, together covering about three-quarters of the sample. Verb-subject-object accounts for around 7 percent, found in Irish, Welsh, Classical Arabic and Māori. The three orders that place the object before the subject are vanishingly rare: verb-object-subject about 2 percent, object-verb-subject and object-subject-verb well under 1 percent each, the latter attested in a handful of Amazonian languages such as Warao and Nadëb. A further 14 percent or so have no dominant order at all. The overwhelming preference for subject-first is one of the few near- universals of human language and is usually attributed to a cognitive preference for mentioning the agent or topic first. Order correlations, first systematised by Joseph Greenberg in his 1963 paper on universals, are more revealing than raw frequencies.
